rules.name: Ability Score Improvement
rules.summary: A universal level-up reward, not a class feature — every class gets it at the same levels.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: An Ability Score Improvement (ASI) lets you raise your ability scores as you level. It is the standard way a character's numbers climb over time: a higher primary ability means better attack and damage rolls, higher save DCs on the effects you force, and stronger saving throws of your own.
This is a base rule of the system. It applies identically to every class, so it lives here in the Rules rather than being printed as a feature on each class sheet.

sections.heading: When you gain one
paragraphs: Every class gains an Ability Score Improvement at 4th level, and again at 8th, 12th, 16th, and 19th level. (Levels beyond 5 are outside the current build scope but the cadence is fixed here so it never has to be re-decided per class.)

sections.heading: What you may do with it
list: Increase one ability score by 2, or
Increase two ability scores by 1 each.
No ability score can go above 20 this way.
If your table uses feats, you may take a feat instead of the score increase.

rules.name: Armor & AC
rules.summary: Armor sets your AC — the number an attack must beat before you even Parry.

sections.heading: AC comes first
paragraphs: Armor Class (AC) is the number an attacker must meet or beat on its attack roll to hit you. Only a hit can be Parried, so armor helps by keeping attacks from reaching the Parry step at all. AC and Parry are two layers of defense, not the same one.

sections.heading: Who wears what
paragraphs: Armour is split by class, and it is split thematically rather than by tradition. Nobody in this company is wearing a suit of anonymous field plate.

Clothing needs no proficiency at all — anyone may wear it — but it is the full casters' entire lane. The Illusionist and the Jester have no armour proficiency whatsoever: they work in robes, coats and costume, and the good stuff is tailored rather than forged.

Light armour covers the performers who live on movement: the Acrobat (armour would defeat the entire point of him), the Juggler, and the Puppeteer. The Doppelganger and the Joker add medium on top — the Joker because he is the one chaos act who genuinely expects to be hit, and the Doppelganger because every Clone he makes shares his Armour Class, so his armour decides how long his whole engine survives. The Sandow alone gets heavy armour and shields.
list: Clothing — Illusionist, Jester (and anyone who wants the look)
Light — Acrobat, Juggler, Puppeteer, Doppelganger, Joker, Sandow
Medium — Doppelganger, Joker, Sandow
Heavy and Shields — Sandow

sections.heading: Armor categories
list: Clothing (e.g. robes): AC 10 + your full Dexterity modifier. Needs no proficiency — the option for casters with no armor training. Same as being unarmored.
Light: base AC + your FULL Dexterity modifier. Quiet and nimble; favors high-Dex characters.
Medium: base AC + Dexterity modifier, but capped at +2. A high-Dex character gains no more than +2 from it.
Heavy: a FIXED base AC — no Dexterity added at all. The best flat AC, but Dexterity never helps; the strongest pieces also require a minimum Strength.
Shield: +2 AC on top of whatever armor (or clothing) you wear.

sections.heading: Armor does not affect Parry
paragraphs: Wearing heavy armor does not make you worse at Parrying. Some classes parry by bracing and absorbing rather than dodging, so armor is never a penalty to it. How good you are at Parrying is set by your class's Parry DC, not by what you wear.

sections.heading: Starter vs bought armor
paragraphs: Not every armor is available at character creation. Starter armor is the basic kit you can begin with: padded, leather, and studded leather; hide and scale; chain mail; and a shield.

Bought armor is a premium upgrade — breastplate, plate, and the like — that you acquire later by purchase or loot, not at creation. A fresh character does not start in plate. Actual prices are left to the DM and the campaign.

sections.heading: Strength requirements
paragraphs: Some heavy armors list a minimum Strength score (Chain Mail 13, Splint and Plate 15). You can still wear the armor without it, but your speed drops by 10 feet while you do. Light and medium armors never have a Strength requirement.

sections.heading: Why some armors look alike
paragraphs: Two armors can share a base AC and differ only in stealth or Strength needs — for example a breastplate and scale mail are both base 14, but the breastplate lets you sneak while scale mail does not. In standard D&D the other differentiator is COST, which is left to your DM here. Once prices are set, the cheaper-but-louder or cheaper-but-weaker option becomes a real budget choice; until then, pick by stealth, Strength, and Dexterity fit.

rules.name: Armor Traits
rules.summary: Every armour carries one always-on trait — the armour equivalent of a weapon's mastery. It is what makes two items with the same AC a real choice, and why the highest-AC item in each tier has none.

sections.heading: Why traits exist
paragraphs: A shopping list where every item is just "one AC worse than the next one up" is not a choice, it is a budget. Worse, the only drawback the old list had was a Stealth penalty, and nothing in this game leans on Stealth hard enough to be worth giving up armour for.

So AC is one axis and the trait is the other. Within a tier, the lower-AC pieces carry the useful traits, and the single highest-AC piece in each category deliberately carries none. That is the trade: wear the best protection, or wear the thing that does something.

sections.heading: The nine traits
list: Warded — advantage on concentration checks, the flat d20 you roll to keep a trick running when you take damage. The reason a caster wears robes rather than nothing.
Deep Pockets — a creature spending its action to snatch one of your Props makes that check with disadvantage.
Supple — advantage on every check and save to escape a grapple, a restraint, or being tied up.
Cushioned — halve the bludgeoning damage you take from falling, from collisions, and from being thrown, including by a friendly Sandow.
Showpiece — advantage on Charisma (Performance) checks: entertaining or holding a crowd with music, dance, acting, storytelling or acrobatics.
Unbound — nothing about it traps your arms, so you can perform a Flourish even while grappled or with only one hand free.
Costumed — advantage on Charisma (Deception) checks to pass as somebody else, or to be taken for part of a crowd or troupe.
Anchored — advantage on saves against being knocked prone and against being moved against your will.
Ironclad — reduce each instance of slashing, piercing or bludgeoning damage you take by 2.

sections.heading: Reading the list
paragraphs: Two pieces at the same AC never share a trait, so there is never a wrong answer that is simply a worse version of the right one. Beasthide Wrap sits a point below the other mediums and pays you back in Cushioned; Serpent-Scale Mail is the best starter medium and pays for it with nothing at all.
Traits do not stack with themselves — a shield's Showpiece and a coat's Showpiece are still just advantage — and advantage from a trait works exactly like advantage from anywhere else.
Every trait name on a card or a sheet is a hover term — point at it and it tells you what it does. You never have to remember this list.

rules.name: Attacks & Damage
rules.summary: Your attacks are your weapons — how to hit and how damage is calculated.

sections.heading: Making an attack
paragraphs: To attack, you take the Attack action and strike with a weapon you are proficient with. Roll a d20 and add your ability modifier and your proficiency bonus; if the total meets or beats the target's Armor Class (AC), you hit.

There is no separate list of 'attacks' for a class — a class attacks with the weapons it is proficient with. Each class page lists those under Attacks, and every weapon's full stats are in the Weapons tab.

sections.heading: Which ability?
paragraphs: Melee weapons normally use Strength; finesse and ranged weapons use Dexterity. Some classes change this: the Puppeteer's Strings of Will lets his Control Wires use Wisdom instead. A class feature always tells you when a different ability applies.

sections.heading: Damage on a hit
paragraphs: A hit deals the weapon's damage die plus the same ability modifier you used to attack. A Rapier (1d8) with a +3 modifier deals 1d8 + 3.

Class features can add more. The Puppeteer's Puppet's Spite adds an extra Wisdom modifier against a strung enemy, so a Control Wires hit — normally 1d4 + Wisdom via Strings of Will — becomes 1d4 + Wisdom + Wisdom on a strung foe.

sections.heading: Where to find damage
paragraphs: Every weapon's damage die, type, properties, and parry profile live on its page in the Weapons tab. Your class page's Attacks section shows the weapons that class actually uses.

rules.name: Appearance & Size
rules.summary: There are no races. Look however you like — it costs nothing and grants nothing. Size is the one exception, and only because two features read it.

sections.heading: There are no races
paragraphs: This game has no racial statlines and is not going to get them. Eight classes were tuned against each other without one, and dropping a second set of bonuses underneath them would quietly undo that work — the first casualty being the only mechanic in the game that cares how big you are.

What you get instead is simpler and more generous: your appearance is entirely yours. Play a dragonborn Joker, a tiefling Jester, a goblin Acrobat, a talking bear who juggles. It costs nothing, grants nothing, and changes no roll. Nobody at the table has to look anything up, and the answer to "can I be..." is always yes.

sections.heading: Size is the exception
paragraphs: Two features in the whole game read a character's size, so size is the one thing your class decides for you rather than you deciding it.

Every class lists the sizes it can be, shown on its own page. For all but one that is Small or Medium. The Sandow — and only the Sandow — may be Medium or Large, because being physically enormous is the entire point of him.

The Sandow's Mighty Build makes him count as one size larger than he is, and he can lay hands on any creature up to that effective size: a Medium Sandow handles Large creatures, and a Large Sandow handles Huge ones. Since the class stops at Large, Huge is the biggest thing anybody in this game can grapple, throw or Crush — Gargantuan is never on the table.
The Impersonator's Borrowed Trick is the other one: his Mimic can only copy a creature of his size or smaller, which is why a Doppelganger is never Large.

sections.heading: So what do you actually pick?
list: Your class — that sets your size options, and everything mechanical about you.
Your size, from the one or two your class allows.
Everything else about how you look, sound, and where you came from — freely, with no mechanical weight at all.

rules.name: Character Creation
rules.summary: How to build one: pick a class, choose your size, assign six ability scores, take your skills and your starter gear. Hit points are taken rather than rolled, and there is no money yet.

sections.heading: The order it happens in
list: Pick a class — it decides almost everything else, including which sizes you may be.
Pick your size from the one or two your class allows. Everything else about your appearance is free and has no mechanical weight.
Assign six ability scores by whichever of the three methods your table uses.
Choose your skill proficiencies from the list your class offers.
Take a starter armour and your class's weapons. Both are free.
At 3rd level, choose your subclass. Some subclasses also hand you extra tricks.

sections.heading: Ability scores: three ways
paragraphs: Use whichever your table prefers — the app supports all three and none is the 'real' one.

The standard array is 15, 14, 13, 12, 10, 8, assigned however you like. Point buy gives you 27 points with the usual costs, and nothing starts above 15. Manual entry is for a table that rolled dice: type the numbers in and the app trusts you.
Your class's primary ability is the number that matters most — it drives your attacks, your save DC, the size of your engine, and how well you Parry. The app highlights it. It never picks for you.

sections.heading: Hit points are taken, not rolled
paragraphs: At 1st level you get the maximum of your hit die plus your Constitution modifier. Every level after that you get the average of the die rounded up, plus your Constitution modifier again — 4 on a d6, 5 on a d8, 6 on a d10, 7 on a d12.
There is no rolling for hit points in this system. A bad roll at level 2 following you for twenty levels is not a decision, it is a tax.

sections.heading: Levels beyond 5
paragraphs: You can build a character up to 20th level, but be aware of what you are getting: every class's features currently stop at 5th. Levels 6 to 20 give you hit points and Ability Score Improvements and nothing else yet.
The range is open so nobody is stopped from playing. Filling it in is work still to come.

sections.heading: There is no money yet
paragraphs: Starter armour and your class's weapons are free at creation. The bought tier exists and is worth reading, but a fresh character does not own any of it — your DM awards it during play.
Prices, a starting purse and everything else about an economy are deliberately not built yet.

rules.name: Parry & Dodging
rules.summary: Active defense — roll to dodge, graze, or overcommit when you are hit.

sections.heading: How Parry works
paragraphs: When an attack roll hits you (beats your AC) and you can see the attacker, you may spend your reaction to Parry. Roll a flat d20 — no modifier is added, because your bonuses are already baked into your Parry DC — and compare the result to your effective Parry DC.

sections.heading: The three outcomes
list: Roll ABOVE your Parry DC: Full Dodge — you take no damage at all.
Roll EXACTLY your Parry DC: Grazing Parry — you take half damage.
Roll BELOW your Parry DC: Overcommitted — you take +50% damage (you committed to the dodge and got caught).

sections.heading: Your Parry DC (lower is better)
paragraphs: Each class has its own Parry Base DC, shown on its class page. Your effective DC for a given attack = class base DC + your weapon's parry modifier + situational modifiers, minus your proficiency bonus (only if you are proficient with the weapon in hand) minus half your defense-ability modifier, with a floor of 3.
So a weapon well-suited to defense, a higher character level, and a good defense ability all push the DC lower, meaning you Full Dodge more often. A ranged or improvised defense pushes it higher.

sections.heading: Cost and timing
paragraphs: Parry costs your reaction, and you have only one reaction per round. A round you spend dodging is a round you cannot make an opportunity attack, and you can fully dodge only one attack per round.

You may Parry any attack you can see that hits you — including an opportunity attack, even one you provoke on your own turn by moving. You cannot Parry while stunned, incapacitated, paralyzed, unconscious, unable to see the attacker, or with no reaction left.

sections.heading: Riposte
paragraphs: On a Full Dodge, some classes can strike back — a riposte. Each class's page describes its own riposte, if it has one.

rules.name: Reaction & Opportunity Attacks
rules.summary: One reaction per round — Parry OR opportunity attack, never both.

sections.heading: One reaction
paragraphs: Every creature — you and monsters alike — has exactly one reaction per round, which refreshes at the start of its own turn. Parrying, making an opportunity attack, and any other reaction all draw from that single reaction.

sections.heading: The tank-or-parry choice
paragraphs: Because you only get one reaction, being hit forces a choice: spend it to Parry now, or take the hit and save your reaction for a bigger threat later in the round.

If several enemies get to attack you in a round — for example, when flashy movement provokes multiple opportunity attacks — you can only Parry one of them. The rest land in full. That exposure is the price of moving boldly around the battlefield.

rules.name: Tricks & Casting
rules.summary: How magic works: there are no spell slots. A trick is a Pledge (at-will), a Turn (free, on a cooldown), or a Prestige (a showstopper that spends your class engine).

sections.heading: There are no spell slots
paragraphs: Magic in the circus is a performance, not a spellbook. You never track slots, you never 'prepare' anything in the morning, and you never lose a spell because you cast something else earlier. A spell here is called a Trick, and a Trick is limited by one of two things: how recently you did it, or how much of your class engine you are willing to burn.
This means your magic runs on the same clock as everyone else's abilities: per combat, not per day. A caster and a Sandow walk into a fight with the same question — what have I got right now?

sections.heading: The three tiers
paragraphs: Every trick is one of three tiers, named for the three acts of a stage illusion. The Pledge shows you something ordinary. The Turn makes it do something extraordinary. The Prestige brings it back, and that is the part the crowd remembers.
list: Pledge — at-will. No cost, no cooldown, use it as often as you like. This is the reliable fallback that should never be your best option, only your always-available one. Damage Pledges grow at levels 5, 11, and 17.

Turn — the workhorse, and most of your repertoire. Most Turns are free and limited only by a cooldown. A full caster (the Illusionist and the Jester) also has a few better Turns that cost some of their engine: those are what you bank the meter for before level 5. A half-caster's Turns are always free, because their engine is already paying for their ordinary attacks.
Prestige — the showstopper. It spends your class engine, it is only available from level 5, and it is meant to be rare and memorable rather than reliable.

sections.heading: Cooldowns: the crowd has Seen it
paragraphs: When you cast a Turn, it becomes Seen — the audience caught the trick, and it will not land again until they have forgotten it. A trick's cooldown is a number of rounds.
At the start of each of your turns, reduce each Seen trick's counter by one. At zero it is ready again. In practice: a cooldown of 2 means you cannot cast that trick again for 2 of your turns.
Outside combat, rounds pass freely — treat a Turn as ready again after about a minute. Utility tricks are effectively at-will when nobody is trying to kill you.
A trick's cooldown is the whole reason it is balanced the way it is. A stronger Turn carries a longer cooldown. There is no upcasting and no spell level: one number does the work.

A Turn that costs engine still has a cooldown. The price does not replace the cooldown - it stacks on top of it, so a costed Turn is limited both by what you can afford and by how recently the crowd saw it.

sections.heading: Prestiges and your engine
paragraphs: A Prestige is the only kind of magic that touches your class engine — your Phantasm, Mirth, Strings, Clones, or Mayhem. It costs a chunk of that meter, priced to eat most of what you have built up.

A full caster has one more use for the meter: a handful of their Turns carry a price of their own. Those sit between the free Turns and the Prestige — good enough to be worth saving up for, cheap enough to cast more than once in a fight. A half-caster never has these; their engine is already spoken for by their own class features.

On top of that price, every Prestige is limited to once per combat, and it resets when the fight ends. Between the two, you cannot open a fight with a Prestige and you cannot do it twice: you have to earn it, and you only get the one.

Note what is still absent — there is no per-day counter and no slot table. Every limit in this system runs on the same per-combat clock as everyone else's abilities, so a caster never walks out of a fight with their real power locked behind a night's sleep.
For the Illusionist and the Jester, casting Turns is what builds the meter, so their whole loop is: cast Turns, bank the engine, unleash the Prestige.

For the Puppeteer, Doppelganger, and Joker, casting builds nothing. Their engines already pay for their core class features, so a Prestige means going without Strings, Clones, or Mayhem for the things those normally buy. That trade is the point.

This holds even when your class's own wording seems to allow it. A Joker gains Mayhem the first time each turn they deal damage — but damage dealt by a Trick never counts, and neither does any roll made as part of one. For these three classes, no trick ever feeds the meter, whatever the trigger says. That is exactly why their Turns are free.

sections.heading: How trick damage grows
paragraphs: A damaging trick is written with a base die, and that die gets bigger as you level - one size up the chain d4 to d6 to d8 to d10 to d12. The number of dice never changes and neither does any modifier; only the die grows. Any die that does this is marked with a small triangle in the app, and hovering it shows you the whole progression.

d12 is the biggest die there is, so a trick that grows past it stops growing sideways and grows in number instead: a 3d8 trick goes 3d10 at level 5, 3d12 at level 11, and 4d12 at level 17. A level-up never leaves your damage exactly where it was.
A full caster (the Illusionist and the Jester) steps up at levels 5, 11, and 17. Their tricks are their main weapon, so their tricks have to keep pace all the way to level 20.

A half-caster (the Puppeteer, the Doppelganger, and the Joker) steps up at levels 5 and 11, and then stops. Their Turns grow alongside a full caster's through the whole early and middle game and end one die size behind. Their Pledges and their Prestige are the exception - those keep the full progression, because an at-will has to stay worth casting and a once-per-combat showstopper has to stay a showstopper.

This is the same shape as the rest of the half-caster deal: you get the real thing, on the same schedule, up to a ceiling the full caster goes past. What you do not also get is a spellcaster's whole damage output - a half-caster's ability modifier is already on every weapon swing they make, so their trick damage never adds it a second time.

sections.heading: Your trick ability
paragraphs: You cast with your class's primary ability — always. The Illusionist uses Intelligence, the Jester and the Joker use Charisma, the Puppeteer uses Wisdom, and the Doppelganger uses Constitution.

This means a trick-user is never split between two stats: the number that makes your class work is the same number that makes your magic work. When a trick calls for a saving throw, the target rolls against your trick save DC.

sections.heading: Components: Patter, Flourish, Prop
paragraphs: A trick lists what you need in order to perform it. Take that away and the trick does not happen — this is how you shut a performer down, and it works on your enemies exactly as well as it works on you.

You never track how many props you have. A performer carries their act with them: casting never uses a prop up, and anything taken or broken during a fight is back in your kit by the end of it. Losing a prop costs you the scene, never the campaign.

A trick you cannot supply a component for simply cannot be cast. There is no partial version and no substitute. Denying one component only shuts off the tricks that need it, so gagging a caster is a real hit but never a full silence — and a class that leans on one prop for two tricks loses both at once, which is exactly why it is worth a DM's action to try.
list: Patter — the voice: the line, the count, the misdirecting joke. Denied while gagged, magically silenced, or otherwise unable to speak. A creature that already has you grappled can use its action to gag you: it makes a Strength (Athletics) check contested by your Athletics or Acrobatics, your choice. You can pull the gag free with an action, or by escaping the grapple.

Flourish — the hands: the pass, the gesture, the reveal. Denied only when you have no free hand at all, whether because they are bound, restrained, or both full. Being grappled does not by itself stop you; a grapple holds you in place, not your wrists. Dropping something to free a hand takes no action.

Prop — a physical object: cards, silks, powder, wire, a coin. A creature within 5 feet can use its action to snatch one, making a Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) check against your passive Perception and taking a prop of its choice on a success. A prop can also be destroyed by anything that would plausibly destroy a small object.

sections.heading: The six disciplines
paragraphs: Tricks are grouped by discipline rather than by the traditional schools of magic. Which disciplines you can learn from depends on your class.

Only three kinds of damage exist in this setting — physical, fire, and psychic — so a discipline's damage follows from what it is: Pyrotechnics burns, and the mind disciplines hurt because the target believes them.
list: Illusion — phantasms, false images, things that are not there. Deals psychic damage.
Mesmerism — hypnosis, charm, the compelling voice. Deals psychic damage.
Legerdemain — sleight of hand, vanishing, misdirection.
Pyrotechnics — flash, bang, fire-eating, the big finish. Deals fire damage.
Animation — objects and bodies moved as though alive. The Puppeteer's alone; no other class learns it.
Fortune — luck, fate, the rigged draw.

sections.heading: Concentration
paragraphs: Some tricks do not end when you finish casting them - an illusion has to be held there. Those say Concentration in their duration, and holding one takes something from you.
You can hold one concentration trick at a time. Casting a second one ends the first, unless a class feature specifically lets you hold more.

Whenever you take damage while concentrating, roll a concentration check: a flat d20, with no modifier of any kind, exactly like a Parry roll. The DC is 10, or half the damage you just took if that is higher. Fail and the trick collapses immediately. Concentration also ends if you are incapacitated, if you die, or if you simply let it go, which takes no action.

If a feature lets you hold two concentration tricks at once, you roll separately for each one when you take damage - a single check never covers both. Holding two illusions is genuinely riskier than holding one, which is the point.

The roll uses no ability modifier on purpose. Every caster here runs on a single stat and a small hit die, and none of them has any reason to invest in Constitution, so tying concentration to it would have made the rule far harsher for them than the equivalent rule is elsewhere. A flat die keeps it equally hard for everybody.

sections.heading: Tricks and the Parry
paragraphs: The Parry answers attack rolls only, and that does not change here. A trick that forces a saving throw cannot be parried — no amount of footwork dodges a phantasm you already believe in. Evading those is the Acrobat's speciality.
A trick that makes an attack roll can be parried like any other attack. Casters are the worst parriers in the circus, and a trick in hand does not change that.

rules.name: Weapon Mastery
rules.summary: Every weapon carries a default combat maneuver any proficient wielder can use — your baseline 'topple / cleave / vex' options, no class feature required.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: Beyond a class's own features, each weapon has a Mastery property: a small maneuver that triggers on your ordinary weapon attacks. Any character proficient with the weapon can use its Mastery — it is the shared combat vocabulary every class has, on top of its engine and features.

A Mastery triggers as part of the attack that sets it off (on a hit, or a miss for Graze), costs no action or resource, and — unless the Mastery says otherwise — applies each time you hit. Where a Mastery forces a save, the DC is 8 + your proficiency bonus + the ability modifier you attacked with.

sections.heading: The masteries
list: Cleave — On a melee hit, make one attack against a second creature within 5 feet of the first and within your reach; on that hit deal the weapon's damage but not your ability modifier. Once per turn.
Graze — On a miss, still deal damage equal to the ability modifier you attacked with (the weapon's damage type).
Nick — When you make the extra attack granted by the Light property, you can make it as part of your Attack action instead of as a bonus action (once per turn).
Push — On a hit, if the target is Large or smaller you can push it up to 10 feet straight away from you.
Sap — On a hit, the target has disadvantage on its next attack roll before the start of your next turn.
Slow — On a hit that deals damage, reduce the target's speed by 10 feet until the start of your next turn.
Topple — On a hit, the target must succeed on a Constitution saving throw (DC = 8 + your proficiency bonus + your attacking ability modifier) or be knocked prone.
Vex — On a hit that deals damage, you have advantage on your next attack roll against that same target before the end of your next turn.

sections.heading: Where to find it
paragraphs: Each weapon lists its Mastery on its own page and in the Attacks table on every class sheet, so you can see at a glance what maneuver your weapon grants.

rules.name: Weapon Properties
rules.summary: What the tags on a weapon (Finesse, Light, Reach, Thrown, Versatile...) actually mean.

sections.heading: Reading a weapon
paragraphs: Every weapon lists a few properties that change how you attack with it. They appear on the weapon's page and in the Attacks table on each class sheet — hover any property name there to see its meaning.

sections.heading: The properties
list: Finesse — Use Strength or Dexterity (your choice) for your attack and damage rolls with it. (A class feature may further change which ability you use — e.g. the Joker uses Charisma.)
Light — Small and easy to handle. Holding a Light weapon in each hand lets you use a bonus action to make one extra attack with the second weapon (two-weapon fighting).
Heavy — Large and unwieldy; Small creatures have disadvantage on attack rolls made with it.
Reach — Adds 5 feet to your reach when you attack with it, and for opportunity attacks.
Thrown — You can throw it to make a ranged attack, using the same ability modifier you would for a melee attack with it.
Two-handed — You need both hands to attack with it.
Versatile — You can use it one- or two-handed; used two-handed it deals the larger 'versatile' damage die shown on its page.
Ammunition — It needs ammunition to make a ranged attack; you draw a piece as part of the attack.
Loading — You can fire only one piece of ammunition when you attack with it, regardless of how many attacks you could normally make.
Special — It has unusual rules described in the weapon's own text.

classes.name: Acrobat
classes.flavor: An aerial rogue who turns falling, swinging, and sprinting into a weapon, never quite where the last swing landed.

proficiencies.skills: Choose two from Acrobatics, Athletics, Performance, Persuasion, Sleight of Hand, and Stealth

classes.parryReskin: You never block the hit at all — a twist of the spine, a mid-air redirect, a heel that was never fully planted turns solid contact into a near-miss.
classes.riposte: On a Full Dodge (your Parry d20 roll comes up strictly above your effective Parry DC), you may spend 1 Momentum to lash back at the triggering attacker for damage of your weapon's type (the lash-back hits automatically, no attack roll). The lash-back die grows as you level, on its own curve: 1d4 at 1st level, 1d6 at 3rd, 1d8 at 5th, 1d10 at 7th, 1d12 at 9th, and 1d20 at 12th. This is a small reward for a clean dodge, not a full attack.

engine.name: Momentum
engine.description: A personal pool of kinetic flow built from constant motion — sprints, spins, swings, and falls turned into finesse. The Acrobat's sole resource.
engine.generation: You build Momentum through motion, and only through motion — no technique that spends Momentum ever also grants it. Gain 1 Momentum (at most once per turn from this movement source) when you move at least 10 feet toward, away from, or around a hostile creature on your turn, or when you take the Dash or Disengage action. You also gain 1 Momentum the first time each turn you use Wall-Run. Trapeze Swing, Strike-and-Vanish, Momentum Strike, Flow State, and Riposte only spend Momentum — they never generate it.
engine.spend: Spend Momentum in 1-point increments, at no action cost beyond the triggering action, to fuel your features (bonus damage, forced movement, extra mobility, or momentum-gated attacks). Unspent Momentum carries over between rounds, but never between fights: you start every combat with 0 Momentum and any left over is lost the moment the fight ends. Momentum is a per-combat currency like every other engine in this system — it is built during a fight and cannot be banked before one.
engine.cap: 5 (L1-4) · 6 (L5+) — Momentum Reserve raises it at 5th level

triggers.label: I moved 10+ ft around a hostile, Dashed or Disengaged

states.label: Hidden (Strike-and-Vanish)
states.why: You are hidden only if you ended with total cover or out of line of sight.

features.name: Momentum
features.description: You gain the Momentum pool, a resource built by moving with speed and spent to fuel your acrobatics and strikes. See your Momentum engine for how it is generated, spent, and capped.
features.narration: You are never quite still. Between one exchange and the next you are rolling a shoulder, shifting your weight, drifting a half-step — and the longer the fight runs, the more of that motion you have stored up and the less anyone can predict where you will be. When you finally spend it, it looks less like effort than like the fight simply going the way you already were.
features.sheetSummary: You gain the Momentum pool. See the Momentum engine for generation, spending, and cap.

features.name: Counterflow
features.description: Turning a blow aside leaves the attacker overextended, and you flow straight into the opening. When you successfully Parry an attack — a Full Dodge or a Grazing Parry, meaning your Parry d20 comes up at least equal to your effective Parry DC — the next attack roll you make before the end of your next turn has advantage. An Overcommitted Parry (a roll below your DC) grants nothing. Because you have only one reaction, this triggers at most once per round.
features.narration: The blade goes past your ribs and you go with it, turning inside its arc while the arm is still committed. For one breath your attacker is stretched out over their own swing with nothing behind it, and you are already reading the gap they left. Everyone watching sees the same thing: they missed, and you noticed.
features.sheetSummary: On a successful Parry (Full Dodge or Grazing Parry), your next attack roll before the end of your next turn has advantage. Overcommitted grants nothing.

features.name: Wall-Run
features.description: As part of your movement, once per turn, you can run up to half your speed along a vertical surface or across something that couldn't normally support your weight (a wall, a taut rope, a row of chairs), provided you end that move on solid ground or something you can grab. This is a signature move: it generates Momentum.
features.narration: You hit the wall at a dead sprint and simply do not stop — three, four strides straight up the brickwork, along the rope, across the backs of the chairs, whatever happens to be there. Gravity gets a vote eventually, but not until you have already landed where you meant to be. The crowd gasps a half-second late, every time.
features.sheetSummary: Movement. Move up to half your speed along a vertical or unsupporting surface; must end on solid footing. Signature move: generates Momentum.

features.name: Trapeze Swing
features.description: As a bonus action and a signature move, you conjure your own rigging from nowhere — a bar, rope, or ring that appears exactly where you need it — and swing up to 30 feet in any direction, ignoring difficult terrain, for 5 feet of movement and 1 Momentum. Your aerial style is flashy, not safe: leaving a creature's reach during the swing provokes opportunity attacks as normal. At the end of the swing you can make one melee weapon attack against a creature within 5 feet. As a flourish, you may spend 3 additional Momentum to make that attack against every hostile creature you pass within 5 feet during the swing instead of just one, each targeted once. You can use Trapeze Swing at most once per turn. (See Flow State at 5th level: on a turn where you use Trapeze Swing, you cannot also trigger Flow State's extra attack.)
features.narration: You reach up and a bar is there — you conjured it out of nothing, and it holds. The room tilts, the floor drops away, and you come down out of the air at a completely different angle from the one everyone was watching. It is not safe and it is not subtle: you go through the fight, not around it, and anything you leave behind gets a free swing at you as you go.
features.sheetSummary: 1 Momentum + 5 ft of movement. Swing up to 30 ft in any direction ignoring difficult terrain; provokes opportunity attacks. Then one melee weapon attack within 5 ft. Flourish (+3 Momentum): make that attack against every hostile you pass within 5 ft. Excludes Flow State this turn.

features.name: Momentum Strike
features.description: When you hit a Large or smaller creature with a melee weapon attack, you can spend 1 Momentum to deal an extra [[1d6]] damage and force it to make a Strength saving throw against your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Dexterity modifier}}. On a failed save, you shove it 5 feet or knock it prone (your choice).
features.narration: You do not so much hit as arrive. Every step of the approach goes into the blow, and the target does not just take it — it gets moved, staggered off its line or put flat on its back with the wind gone out of it. This is the strike that reminds people a tumbler is still hitting them with their entire body weight.
features.sheetSummary: On a melee hit vs Large or smaller. Extra [[1d6]] damage and a Strength save vs your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Dexterity modifier}} or be shoved 5 ft or knocked prone (your choice).

meta.save: Str save vs {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Dexterity modifier}}

features.name: Strike-and-Vanish
features.description: After you hit a creature with a melee weapon attack, you can spend 2 Momentum to move up to half your speed without provoking opportunity attacks and attempt to Hide (per the normal Hide rules — you become hidden only if you end with total cover or out of the target's line of sight). As a flourish, you may spend 2 additional Momentum (4 total) to move your full speed instead of half — a clean disengage out of every enemy's reach (still no invisibility). You can use Strike-and-Vanish once per turn at 3rd level, twice per turn at 5th, three times at 9th, and four times at 12th. This is a signature move.
features.narration: You land the hit and you are already gone — a roll, a shoulder past somebody's hip, a shadow behind a pillar — before the sound of it finishes. Nobody swings at you on the way out, because nobody has worked out which way out you took. If there is anywhere at all to disappear into, that is where you are.
features.sheetSummary: After a melee hit, 1/turn (2 at L5, 3 at L9, 4 at L12). Move half your speed without provoking and attempt to Hide. Flourish (+2 Momentum, 4 total): full speed instead. Signature move.

meta.uses: 1 / turn (2 at L5, 3 at L9, 4 at L12)

features.name: Flowing Reflexes
features.description: A clean parry doesn't end your turn's rhythm — it feeds it. Once per turn, when you successfully Parry an attack (a Full Dodge or a Grazing Parry), you immediately regain your reaction. This regained reaction cannot be spent to Parry again — use it for an opportunity attack or another reaction feature. If your Parry d20 came up a natural 20, you regain two reactions this way instead of one (still none able to Parry again). Any reaction regained this way lasts only until the start of your next turn; if you have not spent it by then, it is lost. Because a Parry still stops only one attack per round, this never makes you a surer dodger — it turns a clean deflection into extra tempo.
features.narration: Turning a blade aside does not cost you your footing — it gives you your footing. The block flows straight back into the rhythm you were already keeping, and by the time the attacker recovers you are somehow ready again, still watching, still loose, as though you were never interrupted at all.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. On a successful Parry you regain your reaction (two on a natural 20). The regained reaction can never Parry and is lost at the start of your next turn.

features.name: Momentum Reserve
features.description: Your reserve of flow runs deeper than another acrobat's. Your Momentum cap increases to 6, and moving through a space occupied by an ally no longer costs extra movement.
features.narration: You have learned to keep more in the tank than a body should. The flow does not run out where it used to, and a friend standing in your way is no longer in your way — you go over, under, or around them without slowing, and they barely feel you pass.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Momentum cap becomes 6. Moving through an ally's space costs no extra movement.

features.name: Aerial Evasion
features.description: You are the one class whose dodging reaches beyond attack rolls. When you are subjected to an effect that allows you to make a Dexterity saving throw for half damage (a fireball, a trap, a breath weapon, or similar area effect), you instead take no damage on a success and only half damage on a failure. This is the sole exception to the rule that saving-throw and area effects can't be Parried.
features.narration: The blast goes off and you are simply not in it. Everyone else is bracing; you are already airborne, twisting through the one seam in the fire where nothing is burning. Even when you misjudge it and clip the edge, you take it moving, rolling out the far side with your coat smoking and your feet under you.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. On an effect allowing a Dexterity save for half damage: no damage on a success, half on a failure. The one exception to Parry answering attack rolls only.

features.name: Flow State
features.description: Once on each of your turns, if you have 3 or more Momentum and have not already gained an attack this turn from Trapeze Swing, you can spend 3 Momentum to make one additional weapon attack as part of the same action you used to make a melee weapon attack. Flow State's extra attack and Trapeze Swing's attack are mutually exclusive within a single turn — at most one of the two can add an attack on top of your normal action-attack, so no single creature can be struck by more than two of your attacks in a turn (your action attack plus one). Trapeze Swing's flourish can still spread additional single hits across several different creatures you pass within 5 feet — that is crowd damage, not focused damage, and it costs Momentum and provokes an opportunity attack from every creature you leave.
features.narration: Somewhere in the middle of the fight it stops being a series of decisions. The dodge is the step is the strike is the next dodge, all one motion, and you land blows in gaps that were not there a moment ago because you are moving faster than anyone is thinking. It never lasts long. While it does, you are the best thing in the room.
features.sheetSummary: One additional weapon attack as part of your melee Attack action. Mutually exclusive with Trapeze Swing's attack in the same turn.

keyStats.note: Most Momentum you can hold at once.

keyStats.note: Best parrier in the roster; lower is better.

classes.name: Doppelganger
classes.flavor: A duplicator and trickster who is never quite where the last blow landed, fighting alongside a handful of semi-real reflections of himself.

proficiencies.skills: Choose two from Acrobatics, Deception, Insight, Perception, Sleight of Hand, and Stealth

classes.parryReskin: A Clone lurches into the blow's path at the last possible instant and takes the hit for you — you were never quite where the blade landed, only where you left an afterimage standing. This is pure narration: it does not change the Parry math already resolved (a Grazing Parry or Overcommitted result still deals whatever damage it deals). For committing Clones to absorb a hit entirely — and losing them if the gamble fails — see Mirror Image.
classes.riposte: On a Full Dodge (your Parry d20 roll comes up strictly above your effective Parry DC), you may create one Clone (see your Clone engine) in an unoccupied space within 5 feet of you, at no action cost and without spending your bonus action. This follows your normal Clone cap — if you are already at your cap, you must let an existing Clone drop first. A small, thematic reward for turning aside a hit clean, not a counterattack.

engine.name: Clones
engine.description: Semi-real mirror-duplicates of yourself, each occupying its own space, wearing your face and frozen in the pose you struck the moment it was made. A Clone is not a combat pet — it never takes actions of its own — it's a body double for a blade, an eye, or your own attacks to work through. A Clone is a snapshot: it copies every benefit affecting you at the instant it is created (advantage, damage riders, a temporary weapon enchantment, and the like) and keeps them for its whole life even if yours end, but it never gains anything applied to you afterward; its AC equals yours and it has no hit points. Clones do not move on their own once placed — you reshape the picture by spawning new Clones where you want them or by using Swap. Because a Clone is a sliver of your own living body rather than an illusion, it is your Constitution — your raw vitality — that powers your duplicates: your Constitution modifier sets their save DCs and is added to any damage a Clone deals — a Mirror Barrage swing, a Mirror Assault strike, a Decoy Detonation burst — in place of the Dexterity your own strikes use, even as your own blades still strike with a duelist’s Dexterity.
engine.generation: Create one Clone, as a bonus action, in an unoccupied space you can see within 30 feet of you; it appears already mimicking your exact appearance and current pose. You also gain a Clone at no action cost via Riposte, and via any other feature that says so. You may never have more Clones active at once than your Clone cap; creating a new one beyond your cap requires an existing Clone to drop first.
engine.spend: Clones aren't spent from one fixed pool all at once — specific features use them in specific ways. Swap teleports you into a Clone's space without destroying it. Mirror Barrage has every Clone in reach make one half-damage attack, without destroying them. Mirror Image commits any number of Clones within 15 feet to a d6 gamble: on a redirect one of them is destroyed and absorbs the hit entirely, and on a failure every Clone you committed is destroyed for nothing. Decoy Detonation destroys a Clone to burst it for damage and knockback. Mirror Assault (5th level) consumes a Clone to deliver an extra attack from its space. A Clone also drops on its own, destroying no other resource, the moment it ends up more than 30 feet from you, the instant you become incapacitated (all your Clones drop at once), or the first time any attack roll succeeds against it — it shares your AC but has no hit points of its own, so one confirmed hit and it's gone. Clones are per-combat like every other engine in this system: every Clone you have drops the moment combat ends, and you enter every fight with none. Clones can never be banked before a fight or carried out of one.
engine.cap: 2 (L1–4) · 4 (L5–8) · 5 (L9+) — proficiency bonus, plus 1 from Hall of Mirrors at 5th level
engine.capFormula: your proficiency bonus, plus 1 from Hall of Mirrors at 5th level

triggers.label: Full Dodge — free Clone from Riposte

states.label: A Mimic is out (Impersonator)
states.why: Once per combat. It copies the creature's AC and one attack, and dies to a single hit.

features.name: Clones
features.description: You gain the Clones engine. As a bonus action, you create one Clone — a semi-real mirror-duplicate of yourself, mimicking your appearance and pose — in an unoccupied space you can see within 30 feet (45 at 5th level). At the instant it appears, a Clone copies your exact state: every benefit currently affecting you (advantage, damage riders, a temporary weapon enchantment, and so on) carries onto the Clone and stays for as long as it exists, even after your own version ends; it does not gain anything applied to you later. You can have up to your Clone cap (your proficiency bonus) active at once; creating one beyond the cap drops an existing Clone. A Clone shares your AC but has no hit points — a single hit destroys it — does not move on its own once placed, and drops if it ends more than 30 feet from you or you become incapacitated. Your other features reposition and spend Clones; see your Clone engine for the full detail.
features.narration: You step sideways and leave someone behind — a second you, wearing your face and frozen in the pose you were just holding. It is not smoke and it is not a picture; it is a sliver of you, breathing, warm, wrong only in that it never blinks. The room stops being sure which one it was watching.
features.sheetSummary: 30 ft (45 at L5). Create one Clone in an unoccupied space; cap = your Clone cap. A Clone copies every benefit on you at that instant and keeps it, shares your AC, has no hit points (one hit destroys it), never moves on its own, and drops if it ends more than 30 ft from you or you become incapacitated.

features.name: Mirror Barrage
features.description: You act, and every reflection acts with you. As a bonus action, each of your Clones that has a creature within its reach makes one weapon attack from its own space against a target it can reach, using your attack roll and whatever weapon and benefits it copied when it was created. On a hit, a Clone deals half its damage, rounded down — and because a Clone strikes with your vitality rather than your aim, it adds your Constitution modifier where your own attack would add Dexterity: roll the weapon's damage die, add your Constitution modifier and any riders the Clone copied, then halve the total. Several Clones positioned around the same target all strike it; Clones spread across different enemies each strike their own. The Clones are not destroyed by attacking — they simply swing. You can use Mirror Barrage once per turn.
features.narration: You swing, and every reflection swings with you, all of them a fraction behind like a badly synced echo. Blades come in from three directions at once from three identical men wearing the same expression. None of them is where the parry goes.
features.sheetSummary: Each Clone with a creature in reach makes one weapon attack from its own space using your attack roll. On a hit it deals half damage, rounded down, adding your Constitution modifier instead of Dexterity. Clones are not destroyed by attacking.

features.name: Mirror Image
features.description: Your Clones double as decoys that can throw themselves into a blow meant for you. When a creature you can see hits you with an attack, then — before you decide whether to Parry — you may commit any number of your Clones within 15 feet of you: they sweep in from wherever they stand and crowd the line of the strike, a wall of identical faces between you and the blade. Committing them costs no action and no reaction. Roll a d6. The more you commit, the better the odds the attacker buries the blow in a reflection: one Clone redirects on a 1 (1-in-6), two on a 1-2 (2-in-6), three on a 1-3 (3-in-6). Three is the ceiling — committing a fourth Clone improves nothing, so never commit more than three. On a redirect, the attack strikes one committed Clone of your choice and destroys it, you take no damage, and your reaction is still free; every other Clone you committed survives and stays where it stopped. On a failure, the gamble costs you everything you put in the way: every Clone you committed is destroyed, the attack lands on you in full, and you may still spend your reaction to Parry it as normal. Clones lost to a failure are not destroyed by an attack roll — nothing that keys off a Clone being struck down triggers for them.
features.narration: You call them in and they come — reflections crowding the line of the blade, shouldering into the space where you were about to be hurt. Sometimes the strike buries itself in one of them and it comes apart like a dropped mirror, and you are untouched behind the falling pieces. Sometimes they crowd in for nothing, shatter all at once, and the blade finds you anyway through the glittering mess.
features.sheetSummary: When a creature you can see hits you and before you decide whether to Parry. Commit any number of Clones within 15 ft, then roll a d6: redirect on a 1 with one committed, 1-2 with two, 1-3 with three (the ceiling — a fourth adds nothing). Redirect: one committed Clone is destroyed, you take no damage, your reaction stays free, the rest survive. Failure: EVERY committed Clone is destroyed, the hit lands in full, and you may still Parry it.

meta.cost: Commit 1-3 Clones (all lost on a failure)

features.name: Swap
features.description: As a bonus action, you may teleport-swap places with one of your Clones within 30 feet of you: you instantly appear in the Clone's space and it instantly appears in yours, each facing however you choose. Neither of you provokes opportunity attacks from this movement, and the Clone itself is not destroyed — it simply continues existing wherever it ends up, still bound by its normal leash and still able to be hit, redirected onto, or spent like any other Clone. You can use Swap once per turn.
features.narration: You and one of your reflections trade places between one heartbeat and the next, with no flash and no sound — just a soft displacement of air and the sudden certainty that you were never standing where the fight thought you were.
features.sheetSummary: Teleport-swap places with one of your Clones. Neither provokes opportunity attacks; the Clone is not destroyed.

features.name: Tricks
features.description: You are a half-caster: your magic is real but it is not the point of you, and it arrives late. From 2nd level you can perform Tricks. You know every trick on the Doppelganger list — a short one — with no preparation and no choosing; each becomes available at the level shown on your class trick ladder, and once available it is always available. Your disciplines are Illusion and Legerdemain. Your trick ability is your Constitution, so your trick save DC is the same number as your Save DC, {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}}, and any trick that makes an attack roll uses {{your trick attack|d20 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}}. Pledges are at-will and Turns cost you nothing but carry a cooldown in rounds; a Prestige spends Clones and can be performed only once per combat. Casting NEVER generates Clones — that is the full casters' loop, not yours, so a Prestige always comes out of the resource your core kit already needs. A damaging Turn of yours also scales more slowly than a full caster's: see the Tricks and Casting rules page.
features.sheetSummary: Half-caster: tricks from level 2. You know the entire Doppelganger list; each unlocks at its listed level. Disciplines: Illusion and Legerdemain. Trick save DC is the same number as your Save DC, {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}}; trick attacks use {{your trick attack|d20 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}}. Pledges at-will, Turns on cooldown, Prestiges spend Clones and are once per combat. Casting never generates Clones.
features.narration: You have spent so long making copies of yourself that you have got good at making copies of other things — a face, a wound, a moment that never happened.

meta.save: Str/Dex/Con/Int/Wis/Cha vs {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}}

features.name: Decoy Detonation
features.description: As an action, you cause one of your Clones to burst in a flash of shattering reflections, destroying it. Because you choose which Clone, you decide where the blast lands — spawn a Clone into a cluster of enemies, or Swap one there, then detonate it. Each creature within 5 feet of that Clone must make a Dexterity saving throw against your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}}. On a failed save a creature takes [[1d6+Con]] psychic damage and is shoved 5 feet straight away from the Clone's space; on a success it takes half as much damage and is not moved. From 3rd level, Splintered Reflexes also lets you trigger Decoy Detonation as a reaction on another creature's turn. You can trigger Decoy Detonation at most once per turn.
features.narration: You let one of them go. The Clone comes apart all at once, not into smoke but into a bursting sphere of edged reflections, and everything close enough is briefly looking at a hundred small pictures of its own surprised face before the shards go through it.
features.sheetSummary: Action (reaction from L3 via Splintered Reflexes). Each creature within 5 ft of the Clone makes a Dexterity save vs your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}}. Fail: [[1d6+Con]] psychic and shoved 5 ft from the Clone's space. Success: half damage, not moved.

meta.save: Dex save vs {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}}

features.name: Flanking Reflection
features.description: When you make a melee weapon attack against a creature that has one of your Clones within 5 feet of it, you have advantage on the attack roll — the creature can't watch both you and your reflection at once. This costs nothing and doesn't destroy the Clone, but requires one to already be positioned correctly; it applies at most once per attack and doesn't stack with other sources of advantage on the same roll.
features.narration: It cannot watch you both. Every time its eyes flick to the copy at its shoulder, its guard drifts a finger's width in that direction — and a finger's width is all you were ever asking for.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Advantage on a melee weapon attack against a creature that has one of your Clones within 5 ft of it. Costs nothing, destroys no Clone, doesn't stack with other advantage.

features.name: Splintered Reflexes
features.description: Your reflections let you answer more than one threat at once. You gain one additional reaction each round, for two total, both refreshing at the start of your turn. This extra reaction can be used only to make an opportunity attack or to activate a Clone feature that costs a reaction — most usefully, it lets you trigger Decoy Detonation on another creature's turn. It can never be used to cast a trick — Parting Shot and any other reaction trick still spend your normal reaction. It can never be used to Parry a second time: you still redirect only one hit per round onto a Clone, so the Acrobat remains the surer dodger. Each reaction is spent once; you choose which threat each one answers.
features.narration: You have stopped answering threats one at a time. Part of your attention lives out in the reflections now, and while one of you is dealing with the blade in front, another is already turning toward the thing coming from the side.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. One additional reaction each round (two total), both refreshing at the start of your turn. The extra one may only make an opportunity attack or activate a Clone feature costing a reaction — never a trick, never a second Parry.

features.name: Mirror Assault
features.description: This is your 5th-level damage step — the Doppelganger's version of Extra Attack, but earned rather than free. Once per turn, when you take the Attack action, if one of your Clones is within 5 feet of your target, you can make one extra weapon attack that strikes from that Clone's space, using your normal attack roll; its damage is the weapon's die plus your Constitution modifier (a Clone's blow draws on your vitality, not your Dexterity). That Clone is then destroyed — it spends itself delivering the blow. Unlike a plain Extra Attack this one is conditional: you need a Clone already positioned next to the target, and it costs you that Clone.
features.narration: You attack from where you are not. The blow lands out of the reflection's space at the same instant yours does, from an angle nobody was covering, and the Clone that threw it is spent in the throwing — it puts everything it had into that one strike and is gone before the body drops.
features.sheetSummary: When you take the Attack action and a Clone is within 5 ft of your target, make one extra weapon attack from that Clone's space: weapon die + your Constitution modifier. That Clone is then destroyed.

features.name: Hall of Mirrors
features.description: Your reflections run deeper and reach farther: your Clone cap increases by 1 (in addition to whatever your proficiency bonus already grants it), and the range on Clone creation, Swap, and a Clone's leash all increase from 30 to 45 feet.
features.narration: The trick has outgrown the room. Your reflections stand further out than they used to and hold together at distances that should have snapped them, until fighting you feels less like facing a man than being surrounded by a hallway of him.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Clone cap +1 on top of your proficiency bonus. Clone creation, Swap, and a Clone's leash all increase from 30 ft to 45 ft.

classes.name: Illusionist
classes.flavor: A stage magician who stopped pretending. What he shows you is not there, and knowing that has never once been enough to save anybody.

proficiencies.skills: Choose two from Arcana, Deception, Insight, Investigation, Performance, and Sleight of Hand

classes.parryReskin: You do not move — the picture of you does. The blade goes through a smear of afterimage while the real body leans a hand's width out of the line, and for one beat nobody in the room including the attacker is sure which was which.
classes.riposte: On a Full Dodge (your Parry d20 roll comes up strictly above your effective Parry DC), the attacker's certainty cracks: it has disadvantage on the next attack roll it makes before the start of your next turn. Having just watched its blade pass through you, it swings at the next one expecting the same. No damage, no action, no Phantasm.

engine.name: Phantasm
engine.description: The banked weight of everything the room currently believes that is not true. Phantasm is not mana — it is credibility. Every trick you perform leaves an impression behind, and the more of them the audience is carrying at once, the more they will accept when you finally ask for something enormous. It is the Illusionist's sole resource, and unlike the part-casters, casting is what builds it: your Turns are not a garnish on a weapon, they ARE the class.
engine.generation: You gain 1 Phantasm each time you cast a FREE Turn — the trick lands, the audience files it away, and you are one step closer to the thing you are really building toward. You gain 1 additional Phantasm the first time each turn a creature fails a saving throw against one of your tricks, because nothing sells the next lie like the last one working. Pledges generate nothing (they are too small to be remembered) and a Prestige generates nothing (it spends the belief rather than building it). **A costed Turn generates nothing** — neither for being cast nor from anything it goes on to do. A trick you paid the meter for never pays part of itself back.
engine.spend: Phantasm is spent three ways, and you have all three from 1st level. **Sell It:** as you cast a trick that forces a saving throw, spend 1 Phantasm to give one target of it disadvantage on that save. **Hold It:** when you fail a concentration check, spend 1 Phantasm to succeed instead. **Costed Turns:** a few of your best Turns carry a price of their own (Waking Nightmare costs 3) — those are the mid-fight payoff you bank the meter for, long before a Prestige is on the table. A Prestige then spends most of what is left. Unspent Phantasm carries over between rounds, but never between fights: you start every combat with 0 Phantasm and any left over is lost the moment the fight ends. Phantasm is a per-combat currency like every other engine in this system — it is built during a fight and cannot be banked before one.

Casting a Turn builds it, and you spend it from 1st level: 1 Phantasm to give one target disadvantage on its save against a trick you are casting (Sell It), 1 Phantasm to turn a failed concentration check into a success (Hold It), and whatever a costed Turn or a Prestige asks for. features.sheetSummary: You gain the Phantasm pool. Spend 1: give one target disadvantage on its save against a trick you are casting. Spend 1: turn a failed concentration check into a success. Costed Turns and Prestiges spend more. Starts every combat at 0.
features.narration: Everything you have made them believe tonight is still in the room, stacked up behind their eyes. You can feel the weight of it, and you can lean on it — to push one more lie past someone's guard, to keep the last one standing when a blade finds you, or to spend the lot on something enormous.

meta.action: Free (as you cast / on a failed check)

features.name: Unreal Assurance
features.description: An illusion of yours is not dispelled merely by being disbelieved. When a creature spends its action to study one of your tricks and determine that it is false, it must succeed on an Intelligence (Investigation) check against your {{trick save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}}. On a failure, nothing happens and it has wasted its action. On a success the illusion is exposed — and it is exposed for EVERYONE, not just for that creature: it says what it has worked out, and the trick stops working on every creature that can perceive it. There is never a state where an illusion is real to some creatures and not others; that is a bookkeeping nightmare at the table and this system does not do it.
features.sheetSummary: A creature must spend its ACTION to study a trick and succeed on an Investigation check vs {{trick save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}}. On a failure it has wasted its action. On a success the trick is exposed for EVERY creature at once, never for that one creature alone.
features.narration: They can decide it is not real. It goes on being there anyway, patient and detailed — until one of them stops fighting long enough to actually look, works out what you have done, and says so out loud. Then the whole room stops believing at once.

meta.save: Investigation check vs {{trick save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}}

features.name: Misdirection
features.description: The audience looks where you tell it to. Once on each of your turns, immediately after you cast a trick, you can move up to 10 feet without provoking opportunity attacks. This movement costs no action and does not use your movement for the turn — every eye in the room is on the thing you just did, and none of them are on your feet.
features.sheetSummary: Immediately after casting a trick: move up to 10 ft without provoking opportunity attacks. Costs no action and doesn't use your movement.
features.narration: The whole room is watching the hand you wanted it to watch. You are somewhere else by the time anybody thinks to check the rest of you.

features.name: Layered Performance
features.description: You can hold two lies in the air at once. You may concentrate on two tricks at the same time instead of one. This does not make either of them safer: when you take damage you roll a separate concentration check for each trick you are holding, against the same DC, so the second illusion is a second thing that can collapse. Casting a third concentration trick ends whichever of the two you choose.
features.sheetSummary: Concentrate on two tricks at once instead of one. When you take damage you roll a SEPARATE concentration check for each, against the same DC. Casting a third ends one of your choice.
features.narration: Two performances running at the same time, in the same room, neither interfering with the other — and both of them leaning on you. Get hit hard enough and you will feel one of them start to go.

features.name: Did You See That?
features.description: You have something to do on other people's turns. When a creature you can see within 60 feet makes an attack roll, you can use your reaction and spend 1 Phantasm to put something in the corner of its eye at exactly the wrong moment: it has disadvantage on that attack roll. You must decide before the roll is made. This uses the same single reaction as your Parry, so on any given round you are choosing between defending yourself and spoiling someone else's swing.
features.sheetSummary: Declared before the roll. A creature you can see has disadvantage on that attack roll. Uses the same single reaction as Parry.
features.narration: Something moves at the edge of its vision — a shape, a face, a flicker of motion that resolves into nothing at all. It is a tenth of a second of doubt, and it arrives while the blade is already moving.

features.name: Illusionist's Discipline
features.description: You commit to a school of the art: choose the Nightmare, Hypnotist, or Trickster discipline. Your choice grants you features at 3rd level.
features.sheetSummary: Choose a discipline: Nightmare, Hypnotist, or Trickster. It grants features at 3rd level.
features.narration: Every illusionist eventually decides what the trick is FOR — the wound that is not there, the mind that agrees with you, or the empty stage where a man used to be standing.

features.name: Vivid Cruelty
features.description: Your phantasms have stopped being pictures. When a creature fails a saving throw against one of your tricks that deals psychic damage, it also has disadvantage on the next attack roll it makes before the end of its next turn. This applies at most once per turn, however many creatures fail.
features.sheetSummary: A creature that fails a save against one of your psychic-damage tricks also has disadvantage on its next attack roll before the end of its next turn.
features.narration: It is not the pain, it is the detail. Whatever you showed them is still there when they blink, and their next swing goes wide because half of them is still looking at it.

features.name: Sustained Illusion
features.description: The performance no longer needs your full attention. Reduce the cooldown of every Turn on your list by 1 round, to a minimum of 1. A trick with a cooldown of 1 is unaffected.
features.sheetSummary: Every Turn on your list has its cooldown reduced by 1 round, minimum 1.
features.narration: The room has stopped requiring you to sell it. You can leave a thing standing and walk away from it, and it holds together on its own long enough for you to start the next one.

classes.name: Jester
classes.flavor: The one member of the company nobody takes seriously, which is exactly why he is still standing. He does not win fights. He decides who does.

proficiencies.skills: Choose two from Acrobatics, Deception, Insight, Performance, Persuasion, and Sleight of Hand

classes.parryReskin: You do not parry so much as make the whole thing look like a bit. A pratfall that happens to take you out of the line, an outraged squawk, the marotte thrown up at the last possible instant — it plays as comedy right up until you are standing and the swing is not.
classes.riposte: On a Full Dodge (your Parry d20 roll comes up strictly above your effective Parry DC), you turn the miss into material: one ally you can see within 30 feet gains {{temporary hit points|equal to your Charisma modifier (minimum 1), set from your stats on your character sheet}}. Nothing lifts a company like watching the fool make an idiot of the thing trying to kill them. No damage, no action, no Mirth.

engine.name: Mirth
engine.description: The room's goodwill, measured. Mirth is what builds when the company is laughing with you and the enemy is not — every joke that lands, every ally who gets back up because you were there, wound up into something you eventually cash in all at once. It is the Jester's sole resource, and like the Illusionist he is a full caster: casting IS the class, so casting is what feeds it.
engine.generation: You gain 1 Mirth each time you cast a FREE Turn. You gain 1 additional Mirth the first time each turn one of your tricks helps an ally — granting them a bonus, temporary hit points, a reroll, resistance, or removing something afflicting them. Pledges generate nothing and a Prestige generates nothing; the Prestige is where the goodwill gets spent, not made. **A costed Turn generates nothing** — neither for being cast nor from anything it goes on to do. A trick you paid the meter for never pays part of itself back.
engine.spend: Mirth is spent three ways, and you have all three from 1st level. **Play It Up:** as you cast a trick that helps an ally, spend 1 Mirth to double what that ally gets from it — the temporary hit points, the bonus die, the number of rerolls. **Heckle:** Heckler's Timing costs 1 Mirth and your reaction, and either softens a blow or spoils a saving throw. **Costed Turns:** a few of your better Turns carry a price of their own (Killing It costs 2) — the mid-fight payoff you bank the meter for, long before a Prestige is on the table. A Prestige then spends most of what is left. Unspent Mirth carries over between rounds, but never between fights: you start every combat with 0 Mirth and any left over is lost the moment the fight ends. Mirth is a per-combat currency like every other engine in this system — it is built during a fight and cannot be banked before one.

features.narration: Everything you do is delivered to the room rather than aimed at a person — a line, a gesture, a bit of business with the marotte — and somewhere in the laugh, the actual work gets done.
