See your Mirth engine for generation and cap.
features.sheetSummary: You gain the Mirth pool. Spend 1: double what one ally gets from a supporting trick you are casting. Spend 1 (+ your reaction): Heckler's Timing. Costed Turns and Prestiges spend more. Starts every combat at 0.
features.narration: You can hear it building — the company loosening up, the fight turning into a show — and you have learned exactly when to spend it and on whom.

meta.action: Free (as you cast / with your reaction)

features.name: Never the Target
features.description: Nobody's first instinct is to kill the clown. Once per round, when a hostile creature that can see both you and an ally within 5 feet of you makes an attack roll against you, it has disadvantage on that roll — it does the arithmetic everyone does and decides the armed one is the problem. This costs no action and no reaction, and it refreshes at the start of each of your turns.
features.sheetSummary: Refreshing at the start of your turn. When a hostile that can see both you and an ally within 5 ft of you attacks you, it has disadvantage on that roll.
features.narration: It looks at you, then at the armed and serious person beside you, and does the arithmetic everyone does. You are not a threat. You are a distraction with bells on. It swings at you like it is swatting something.

features.name: Play to the Room
features.description: You can carry a joke to more than one person. When you cast a Turn that targets a single ally, you may target a second willing ally within 30 feet of the first with the same effect. You can do this {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} times per combat. This never doubles a trick aimed at an enemy.
features.sheetSummary: {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} uses per combat. A Turn that targets a single ALLY may also target a second willing ally within 30 ft of the first. Never applies to a trick aimed at an enemy.
features.narration: You deliver it to the pair of them at once, the way a good line is thrown to two people on opposite sides of the stage. Both of them get it. Both of them straighten up.

features.name: Heckler's Timing
features.description: Your interruptions land where they hurt, but only in the two places a heckle can actually reach. Spend your reaction and 1 Mirth to aim it at one creature within 30 feet that can hear and understand you, choosing one of the applications below. **It never touches an attack roll or an ability check** — you cannot talk someone out of a swing they have already started.
features.sheetSummary: Target must hear and understand you. Choose one application below. Never applies to an attack roll or an ability check. Uses the same single reaction as Parry.
features.narration: You wait for the exact instant before it commits and then say the one thing guaranteed to get in. It is petty, it is unfair, and the wince is worth every penny.

options.name: Take the sting out (damage)
options.effect: When the creature deals damage, reduce that damage by 1d6, to a minimum of 0. Declared after the damage is rolled.

options.name: Spoil the moment (saving throw)
options.effect: When the creature makes a saving throw, it subtracts 1d6 from the roll. Declared before the roll is made.

features.name: Jester's Repertoire
features.description: You settle into the kind of fool you are: choose the Fatemonger, Ringleader, or Buffoon repertoire. Your choice grants you features at 3rd level.
features.sheetSummary: Choose a repertoire: Fatemonger, Ringleader, or Buffoon. It grants features at 3rd level.
features.narration: Every fool works out eventually which part of the act is really his — the rigged odds, the room in his hand, or the sheer punishing stupidity of refusing to fall down.

features.name: The Show Must Go On
features.description: You do not let a performance end badly. When an ally you can see within 30 feet is reduced to 0 hit points, you can use your reaction to keep them upright: they drop to 1 hit point instead. You can do this once per combat.
features.sheetSummary: When an ally you can see drops to 0 hit points, they drop to 1 instead.
features.narration: You are already talking before they hit the ground — some rubbish about the second act, delivered at a shout — and somehow it is enough to keep their feet under them for one more round.

features.name: Practised Patter
features.description: The material is worn smooth from use. Reduce the cooldown of every Turn on your list by 1 round, to a minimum of 1. A trick with a cooldown of 1 is unaffected.
features.sheetSummary: Every Turn on your list has its cooldown reduced by 1 round, minimum 1.
features.narration: You have done all of this a thousand times, in worse rooms, to harder crowds. The timing no longer requires thought — it simply comes round again sooner.

classes.name: Joker
classes.flavor: A chaos menace with a deck of razor cards and a grin that never quite fits the moment — he wins by making sure no one, least of all himself, knows what happens next.

attackAbility.note: Sleight of Hand — Charisma on finesse weapons

proficiencies.skills: Choose two from Acrobatics, Deception, Intimidation, Performance, Persuasion, and Sleight of Hand

classes.parryReskin: A lunatic, last-second contortion — a mad twist of the spine or a limb bent the wrong way at the worst possible instant. He never dodges the sane way, and the crowd can never tell whether it was skill or dumb luck.
classes.riposte: On a Full Dodge (your Parry d20 roll comes up strictly above your effective Parry DC), the triggering attacker must succeed on a Charisma saving throw against your gambit DC or suffer a minor mishap: its next attack roll before the start of your next turn is made with disadvantage.

engine.name: Mayhem
engine.description: A small pool of chaotic energy built from doing risky, unpredictable things in a fight and spent to draw Wild Cards and fuel Gambits. The Joker's sole resource — deliberately kept small so its swings stay bounded rather than build into a snowball.
engine.generation: Gain 1 Mayhem the first time each turn you deal damage to a creature, AND gain 1 Mayhem the first time each turn you take damage, AND gain 1 Mayhem the first time each turn you roll a natural 1 or a natural 20 on an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw — three separate sources, each capped at once per turn (all three triggering in the same turn grants 3 Mayhem total; a source that already triggered this turn grants no more). This works from 1st level. None of these sources ever trigger off a Trick: damage you deal with a Trick, and rolls you make as part of one, generate no Mayhem. Your Tricks are free precisely because they don't feed the meter.
engine.spend: Spend Mayhem in 1-point increments, at no action cost beyond the triggering feature, to draw Wild Cards, fuel your Gambits, and pay for your other Mayhem-keyed features. Unspent Mayhem carries over between rounds, but never between fights: you start every combat with 0 Mayhem and any left over is lost the moment the fight ends. Mayhem is a per-combat currency like every other engine in this system — it is built during a fight and cannot be banked before one.

features.name: Mayhem
features.description: You gain the Mayhem pool, a resource built from doing risky, chaotic things in a fight and spent to fuel your Wild Cards and Gambits. See your Mayhem engine for exactly how it is generated, spent, and capped.
features.narration: Every stupid, reckless, funny thing you do in a fight winds you tighter. You are grinning too much for someone bleeding this freely, and the pressure of it builds behind your teeth until you spend it on something nobody could have planned for.
features.sheetSummary: You gain the Mayhem pool. See the Mayhem engine for generation, spending, and cap.

features.name: Wild Talent
features.description: Your chaos answers your personality, not your hands: you use your Charisma modifier, instead of Strength or Dexterity, for attack and damage rolls you make with a finesse weapon you're proficient with (your Razor Cards, Harlequin's Cane, or Dagger). Any saving throw a Joker feature or Wild Card forces on a creature uses your {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}}.
features.narration: You do not fight like someone who trained. You fight like someone talking — the whole thing runs on nerve and timing and the absolute confidence that the card will go where you said it would, and somehow it does.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Use your Charisma modifier for attack and damage rolls with a finesse weapon you're proficient with. Every save a Joker feature or Wild Card forces uses your {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}}.

features.name: Wild Card
features.description: As a bonus action, spend 1 Mayhem to draw a Wild Card: roll a d8 and immediately resolve the matching result below, with no further action needed. Any saving throw listed is a Charisma saving throw against your gambit DC. Drawing costs a bonus action and 1 Mayhem, so it happens at most once per turn.
features.narration: You draw off the top without looking and let the deck decide what happens next. So does everyone else. The card turns over, the room finds out together, and for one second you are as surprised as anybody — you just hide it better.
features.sheetSummary: Roll a d8 and resolve the matching result. Saves listed are Charisma saves vs {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}}.

options.name: Ace Up the Sleeve
options.effect: You have advantage on the next attack roll or saving throw you make before the end of your next turn.

options.name: Marked Card
options.effect: The next attack you hit with before the end of your next turn deals an extra [[1d6]] damage of that weapon's damage type.

options.name: Contagious Cackle
options.effect: Choose one creature you can see within 30 feet; it must succeed on a saving throw or its next attack roll before the start of your next turn is made with disadvantage.

options.name: Quick Vanish
options.effect: Until the end of your turn your speed increases by 10 feet, and you don't provoke opportunity attacks when you move away from a hostile creature this turn.

options.name: Second Wind
options.effect: You regain [[1d4]] + your Charisma modifier hit points (minimum 1).

options.name: Wild Swap
options.effect: The deck turns on you for a moment — choose one hostile creature within 30 feet of you; it has advantage on the next attack roll it makes against you before the start of your next turn.

options.name: Static Shock
options.effect: A spark of raw chaos jumps back through your own hand and you take [[1d4]] psychic damage.

options.name: Encore
options.effect: If you have at least 1 Mayhem remaining, you may immediately spend it to draw again, rerolling on this table and resolving only the new result (this draw itself does nothing); if you have no Mayhem left, this draw has no further effect.

features.name: Chaotic Parry
features.description: Once per turn when you Parry, after seeing the result, you may spend 1 Mayhem to reroll your Parry d20 — you must use the new roll, even if it is worse. Every Parry of yours narrates as a lunatic, last-second contortion rather than a clean block; the crowd can never tell whether it was skill or dumb luck.
features.narration: Your defence is not a block. It is a stumble, a duck that turns into a spin, a hand thrown up at the last possible instant — and when it looks like it went badly you simply refuse the result and flail your way into a better one. Nobody can tell whether you meant any of it. Neither can you.
features.sheetSummary: After seeing your Parry result, reroll the Parry d20. You must use the new roll even if it is worse.

features.name: Trickster's Luck
features.description: The deck looks after its own. {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} times per combat, when you roll below your effective Parry DC (an Overcommitted result), you can treat that Parry as a Grazing Parry instead — taking half damage rather than +50%. You decide after seeing the roll. This doesn't change your Parry DC, only how badly a failed one lands.
features.narration: The blow that should have opened you up somehow only skims. A boot slips, a lamp swings, the floor is fractionally where it needed to be — the deck looks after its own, and you take the graze with an expression that suggests you arranged it.
features.sheetSummary: Free, {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} times per combat. Treat an Overcommitted Parry as a Grazing Parry instead (half damage rather than +50%). Decided after seeing the roll; your Parry DC is unchanged.

features.name: Tricks
features.description: You are a half-caster: your magic is real but it is not the point of you, and it arrives late. From 2nd level you can perform Tricks. You know every trick on the Joker list — a short one — with no preparation and no choosing; each becomes available at the level shown on your class trick ladder, and once available it is always available. Your disciplines are Legerdemain, Fortune, and Pyrotechnics. Your trick ability is your Charisma, so your trick save DC is the same number as your Gambit DC, {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}}, and any trick that makes an attack roll uses {{your trick attack|d20 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}}. Pledges are at-will and Turns cost you nothing but carry a cooldown in rounds; a Prestige spends Mayhem and can be performed only once per combat. Casting NEVER generates Mayhem — that is the full casters' loop, not yours, so a Prestige always comes out of the resource your core kit already needs. A damaging Turn of yours also scales more slowly than a full caster's: see the Tricks and Casting rules page.
features.sheetSummary: Half-caster: tricks from level 2. You know the entire Joker list; each unlocks at its listed level. Disciplines: Legerdemain, Fortune, and Pyrotechnics. Trick save DC is the same number as your Gambit DC, {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}}; trick attacks use {{your trick attack|d20 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}}. Pledges at-will, Turns on cooldown, Prestiges spend Mayhem and are once per combat. Casting never generates Mayhem.
features.narration: You start doing things with the cards that the cards do not really do. Nobody in the company can tell where the sleight stops and the magic starts, and you have never volunteered the answer.

features.name: Gambit
features.description: As a bonus action, spend 1 Mayhem to attempt a Gambit — a small, rule-bending trick. Choose one:
features.narration: You try something the fight has no rule for. It is fast, it is cheap, it is beneath you, and the moment it works everyone watching hates that it worked.
features.sheetSummary: Choose one Gambit below. Charisma save vs {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}}.

options.name: Switcheroo
options.effect: Choose one creature you can see within 30 feet of you; you and it instantly swap positions, each appearing in the other's space, and neither of you provokes opportunity attacks from the move (each of you must be able to occupy the other's space). Close on a target, drag a dangerous foe off a fragile ally and take its place yourself, or trade spots with an ally to slip out of a bad one. A willing creature swaps automatically; an unwilling creature can refuse by succeeding on a Charisma saving throw against your gambit DC (on a success, neither of you moves).

options.name: Jinx
options.effect: Choose one creature you can see within 30 feet of you and stack the deck against it. The first attack roll or saving throw it makes before the start of your next turn, it must roll twice and use the lower result. Unlike your other tricks, this also spoils a saving throw — set it up on your turn before an ally's spell or your own gambit lands. A hostile creature can shrug the jinx off by succeeding on a Charisma saving throw against your gambit DC when you declare it (on a success, the jinx has no effect).

options.name: Fortune's Favor
options.effect: Choose one ally within 30 feet of you; the next attack roll or saving throw it makes before the start of your next turn is made with advantage.

meta.save: Cha save vs {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}}

features.name: Loaded Deck
features.description:
The first time each turn you hit a creature with a finesse weapon you're proficient with, you can spend 1 Mayhem to deal an extra [[1d6]] damage of that weapon's damage type.

**On a critical hit — whether it came up naturally on a 20 or was forced by Ace in the Hole — everything doubles together.** You double the weapon's damage dice as normal AND you double Loaded Deck's extra dice, because they are damage dice on the same attack. A natural 20 also means Loaded Deck costs you no Mayhem at all: the deck was already loaded.
features.narration: The card that leaves your hand is heavier than it has any right to be. It goes in past the guard at an angle a card should not hold, and the wound it opens is much worse than the sound it made.
features.sheetSummary: On your first hit of the turn with a finesse weapon you're proficient with: extra [[1d6]] damage of that weapon's type. On ANY critical hit — natural 20 or forced by Ace in the Hole — the weapon's dice AND Loaded Deck's dice are both doubled. On a natural 20 it also costs no Mayhem.

features.name: Contagious Panic
features.description: As an action, spend 2 Mayhem to unravel the nerve of up to two creatures you can see within 30 feet of you and within 10 feet of each other. Each must succeed on a Charisma saving throw against your gambit DC or have disadvantage on the next attack roll it makes before the start of your next turn. This deals no damage and imposes no condition beyond that single disadvantage — a moment of dread, not a stun.
features.narration: You say the one thing nobody in the room wanted said out loud, and you say it while smiling. Two of them catch it at once — the confidence goes out of their arms, and for the next few seconds neither is quite committing to anything.
features.sheetSummary: Up to 2 creatures within 10 ft of each other. Charisma save vs {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}} or disadvantage on the target's next attack roll before the start of your next turn. No damage, no other condition.

meta.save: Cha save vs {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}}

features.name: Full House
features.description: When you spend Mayhem to draw a Wild Card, you may spend 1 additional Mayhem (2 total) to draw two cards instead of one. If you do, resolve only one of the two results — your choice — and discard the other; you never resolve both at once.
features.narration: You draw two and fan them out where only you can see. Whatever the second card was, nobody will ever know: you let it fall, play the one you like, and act as though that was the only card there ever was.
features.sheetSummary: Special, +1 Mayhem (2 total) when drawing a Wild Card. Draw two cards and resolve only one of your choice; the other is discarded.

features.name: Ace in the Hole
features.description: Once per turn, when you hit a creature with an attack using a finesse weapon you're proficient with, you can spend 2 Mayhem to treat the attack as a critical hit, doubling its damage dice as normal for a critical hit. This doesn't stack with an attack that was already a natural-20 critical hit — Ace in the Hole turns an ordinary hit into a showstopper, it doesn't make an already-crit hit bigger. Forcing the deck this hard leaves you exposed: until the start of your next turn, attack rolls against you have advantage.
features.narration: You force it. The strike goes exactly where nothing should be able to go, perfect and vicious and completely beyond what luck owed you — and the deck collects immediately. For the next few seconds you are wide open and everyone can see it, including you.
features.sheetSummary: On a hit with a finesse weapon you're proficient with. Treat the attack as a critical hit (damage dice doubled). Doesn't stack with a natural-20 crit. Until the start of your next turn, attack rolls against you have advantage.

keyStats.label: Gambit DC
keyStats.note: Save DC for Wild Cards, Gambits, and every other Joker effect that forces a save. This same number is your trick save DC.

keyStats.label: Mayhem Cap
keyStats.note: Most Mayhem you can hold at once.

keyStats.label: Parry Base DC
keyStats.note: Dead centre of the roster; lower is better.

classes.name: Juggler
classes.flavor: The circus juggler as duelist — a constant cascade of knives, weighted orbs, and clubs, every one a weapon he can loose or keep. He fights in bursts: hurl a storm of thrown steel and stand exposed, or hold a few back to knock the answer aside.

proficiencies.skills: Choose two from Acrobatics, Performance, Sleight of Hand, Insight, and Deception

classes.parryReskin: You don't dodge — you deflect, knocking an incoming blow aside with an implement still in your hand. The more of your set you have already hurled, the less you have left to guard with; empty-handed, all you can do is wait to catch them back at the start of your next turn.
classes.riposte: On a Full Dodge (your Parry d20 comes up strictly above your effective Parry DC), you catch the blow on a held implement and flick it back in the same motion: the triggering attacker takes [[1d4]] damage of that implement's type, no attack roll and no cost beyond the Parry. You keep the implement — this is a deflection, not a throw.

engine.name: Juggle Set
engine.description: You are always juggling a set of light implements — throwing knives, weighted orbs, clubs. They are your ammunition and your guard at once. You never buy, gather, or track them: at the start of each of your turns you catch your whole set back to full. On your action you decide how many to throw; whatever you keep in hand is what you can Deflect with. This baseline is shared by every Juggler from 1st level; your subclass (chosen at 3rd level) shapes what your implements do.
engine.generation: At the start of each of your turns your set refills to full — you catch every implement back into the cascade, thrown or not. There is no other way to gain or lose implements; they are never spent for good.
engine.spend: On your Attack action you throw any number of implements, from 0 up to your Set Size, as your Barrage. Each implement thrown leaves your hand until your set refills, and every one you have thrown worsens your Deflect (with none in hand you cannot Parry at all). Nothing carries between fights here either — but nothing needs to. Your Set refills to full at the start of each of your turns, so however a fight ended, your first turn of the next one opens with every implement back in hand.
engine.capFormula: proficiency bonus + 1 (+2 more from Grand Cascade at L5)

states.label: Mark on a creature (Impalement)
states.why: One at a time; lasts until the end of your next turn.

features.name: Juggle Set
features.description: You gain the Juggle Set — the ring of implements you always keep in the air. See your engine for exactly how it refills, how many you hold (your Set Size), and how throwing them feeds your Barrage and drains your Deflect. Your Set Size is 3 at 1st level and grows as you gain levels.
features.narration: The cascade never stops. Clubs, knives, weighted orbs — whatever the act calls for, going up and coming down in a loop you have not consciously thought about in years. It is a weapon rack and a guard and a performance all at once, and it only exists while it is moving.
features.sheetSummary: You gain the Juggle Set. Set Size is 3 at 1st level and grows with level. See the engine for refills, Set Size, and how throwing feeds Barrage and drains Deflect.

features.name: Barrage
features.description: When you take the Attack action, you loose your Barrage instead of making a normal attack: choose any number of implements from 0 up to your Set Size and throw them at targets you can see within normal thrown range (20 feet, or up to 60 at disadvantage). Each thrown implement is a separate ranged {{attack roll|d20 + Dexterity modifier + proficiency bonus}}. On a hit, the FIRST of your implements to land each turn deals [[1d4+Dex]]; every implement that hits after that deals only its [[1d4]] die, no ability modifier — a barrage is a flurry, not a dozen full-power strikes. Any Weapon Mastery your implements carry (such as Topple or Slow) triggers at most once per Barrage, however many implements hit. You may split them across different targets or pile them all onto one. Throwing 0 is a real choice — you make no attack but keep your full set in hand for defense (see Deflect).
features.narration: You break the pattern and throw. One, three, everything — the cascade comes apart into a line of implements crossing the room in a stream, and the only question you actually had to answer was how much of your guard you were willing to put in the air.
features.sheetSummary: Attack action. Throw 0 up to your Set Size implements at targets within 20 ft (60 at disadvantage). Each is a separate ranged {{attack roll|d20 + Dexterity modifier + proficiency bonus}}. The first implement to hit each turn deals [[1d4+Dex]]; every later hit deals [[1d4]] with no modifier. Weapon Mastery triggers at most once per Barrage. Throwing 0 keeps your full set for Deflect.

features.name: Flourish
features.description: The more of your set you commit to a Barrage, the flashier the trick — but you get only ONE flourish per turn, decided by how many implements you throw. You gain the single benefit for your throw count, not the lower ones (throw 2 and you get the second effect only, not the first):
features.narration: The bigger the throw, the bigger the trick around it — a spin, a blind catch behind the back, a moment held for the room. You get one flourish out of it, and which one you get depends entirely on how much you committed.
features.sheetSummary: Part of your Barrage, one tier per turn. You gain only the single benefit matching how many implements you threw, not the lower tiers.

options.name: Throw 1
options.effect: Pinpoint — you have advantage on that attack roll. A single aimed throw made with your guard still up (you keep almost your whole set for Deflect).

options.name: Throw 2
options.effect: Off-Balance — a creature you hit with an implement this turn has disadvantage on its next attack roll before the start of your next turn.

options.name: Throw 3 or more
options.effect: Showstopper — for the rest of this turn your thrown implements score a critical hit on a roll of 19 or 20, the all-in flurry finding every gap. Committing three or more implements badly weakens your Deflect this round (and empties your hands entirely at low levels), so the crit-fishing costs you your guard.

features.name: Deflect
features.description: Your Parry is a deflection made with an implement still in hand, so how well you can do it depends on how many you are still holding. Your effective Parry DC is your base of 12 while you hold your full set, and it worsens by 1 for each implement you have thrown and not yet caught back — that is, +1 for each one short of a full set. If you are holding no implements at all, you cannot Parry until your set refills at the start of your next turn. Because the set refills every turn, this resets each round: a turn you throw everything is a turn you stand defenseless, and a turn you hold some back keeps your guard up at a worse DC. Deflecting still costs your reaction like any Parry.
features.narration: You do not block with your hands, you block with whatever is passing through them. A club comes down and something of yours is there to meet it — provided anything of yours is still in the air. Empty-handed, there is nothing to do but watch it land.
features.sheetSummary: Your effective Parry DC is 12 while holding a full set, worsening by 1 for each implement thrown and not yet caught back. Holding none means you cannot Parry at all until your set refills at the start of your next turn. Costs your reaction like any Parry.

features.name: Nimble Cascade
features.description: A juggler never plants his feet. As a bonus action on your turn, you can move up to half your speed, and that movement doesn't provoke opportunity attacks. Open the range before you empty your set, or slip away on a turn you're left defenseless.
features.narration: You keep the pattern going with your hands while your feet leave. It is the oldest trick in the act: nobody watches the man's boots when his hands are doing that.
features.sheetSummary: Move up to half your speed without provoking opportunity attacks.

features.name: Ricochet
features.description: Your implements carom off their targets. Once on each of your turns, when a thrown implement hits a creature during your Barrage, you can have it ricochet outward from that target: make a separate ranged attack roll against every other creature you can see within 15 feet of it, and on each hit the implement deals [[1d4+Dex]] damage (rolled separately for each). Only ONE implement ricochets per turn, no matter how many you throw — so a full 3-implement Barrage still gets a single ricochet. The ricochet is a free bonus of an implement you already threw: it doesn't cost you an implement or further worsen your Deflect.
features.narration: The implement does not stop where it hit. It skips off at an angle you called before you threw and goes on to find someone else, then someone after that, still spinning.
features.sheetSummary: Part of your Barrage, 15-ft burst. When a thrown implement hits, make a separate ranged attack against every other creature within 15 ft of that target; each hit deals [[1d4+Dex]]. Only one implement ricochets per turn. Costs no implement and doesn't worsen Deflect.

features.name: Trick Shot
features.description: You don't just throw hard — you throw smart, reading angles and gaps mid-cascade. Once on each of your turns you can designate ONE implement in your Barrage as a Trick Shot — never more than that single implement, no matter how many you throw. On a hit, in addition to its normal damage, the target must succeed on a saving throw against your {{Trick Shot DC|6 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}} or suffer one effect of your choice (the save ability depends on the effect):
features.narration: You throw at what everyone is looking at and hit something else — a wrist, a knee, the buckle of a strap. One implement out of the stream does something the others were only ever a distraction for.
features.sheetSummary: Part of your Barrage. Designate one implement as a Trick Shot. On a hit, in addition to damage, the target makes a save vs your {{Trick Shot DC|6 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}} or suffers one effect of your choice (the save ability depends on the effect).

options.name: Blind
options.effect: An orb bursts across its eyes — Constitution save or blinded until the end of its next turn.

options.name: Trip
options.effect: A club takes its legs — Strength save or knocked prone.

options.name: Disarm
options.effect: A knife to the knuckles — Strength save or it drops one item it is holding (your choice), landing at its feet.

options.name: Pin
options.effect: The implement staples a limb in place — Dexterity save or its speed becomes 0 until the end of its next turn.

meta.save: vs Trick Shot DC (Int)

features.name: Grand Cascade
features.description: Your cascade widens. Your Set Size increases by 2 — it is now your proficiency bonus + 3 — so you juggle, hold, and can throw that many more implements each turn. Every extra one you keep still shores up your Deflect, and every extra one you throw still feeds your Barrage, Ricochet, and Trick Shot.
features.narration: The pattern widens. There is more in the air than a person should be able to track, and you are not tracking it — you stopped needing to a long time ago.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Set Size increases by 2, becoming your proficiency bonus + 3.

features.name: Chain Reaction
features.description: Keep the show going. Once per combat, you can choose to make your Ricochet chain: after it sprays its targets, pick one creature it hit and the implement caroms off and ricochets a second time from that creature's space — a separate ranged attack against every other creature you can see within 15 feet of it, dealing [[1d4+Dex]] on each hit, exactly like Ricochet. You decide when to trigger it; it does not require dropping a target.
features.narration: You keep it going past the point where it should have fallen. The implement caroms, caroms again, and by the time it finally comes down the crowd is on its feet and half the room is bleeding.
features.sheetSummary: Part of your Barrage, 15-ft burst. After your Ricochet resolves, pick one creature it hit; the implement ricochets a second time from that creature's space, dealing [[1d4+Dex]] on each hit. You choose when to trigger it.

keyStats.label: Set Size
keyStats.formula: proficiency bonus + 1 (Grand Cascade adds +2 more from L5)
keyStats.note: How many implements you hold and can throw each turn.

keyStats.label: Implement Damage
keyStats.note: First implement to hit each turn adds Dex; the rest deal the die only. Die scales at L5/11/17.

keyStats.label: Trick Shot DC
keyStats.note: Save DC for Trick Shot effects and your subclass's forced saves (from L3). Modest in practice since Int is a secondary stat.

keyStats.label: Parry Base DC
keyStats.note: At full hands; +1 per implement thrown, none held = no Parry. Lower is better.

classes.name: Puppeteer
classes.flavor: A marionettist who never means to enter the fight himself — a web of near-invisible wire turns foes into puppets and allies into partners, moved exactly where the show demands.

proficiencies.skills: Choose two from Deception, Insight, Intimidation, Performance, Persuasion, and Sleight of Hand

classes.parryReskin: You are no blocker at all — a curtain of near-invisible wire snaps up between you and the blow at the last instant, trying to deflect what your own body never could. It is a last resort, not a specialty: your effective Parry DC runs the worst in the roster, so a clean Full Dodge is rare, and more often the wire only barely turns aside what it can't fully stop.
classes.riposte: On a Full Dodge (your Parry d20 roll comes up strictly above your effective Parry DC), you may attach a String to the triggering attacker at no action cost and without spending your bonus action. This follows your normal String cap — if you are already at your cap, you must detach an existing String to make room. A small, thematic reward for a clean dodge, not a counterattack.

engine.name: Strings
engine.description: Lengths of near-invisible wire you fix to creatures around you. A String is not spent like currency — it is an attachment that stays in place, keying your control features to whatever it's tied to, until you choose to let go of it or something forces you to.
engine.generation: Attach a String to a creature you can see within 60 feet as a bonus action, or automatically at no action cost when you hit a creature with your Control Wires. You may never have more Strings attached at once than your String cap; attaching a new one beyond your cap requires detaching an existing String first (no action).
engine.spend: Strings aren't consumed to use your control features — they are the prerequisite for them. Manipulate, Tangle, Disrupting Pull, Guiding Pull, and Grand Marionette all require a String already attached to the target; using them doesn't remove the String. A String stays attached until you detach it (no action), the creature moves beyond your 60-foot leash range, or you become incapacitated, in which case all of your Strings snap at once. Strings are per-combat like every other engine in this system: every String you have snaps the moment combat ends, and you enter every fight with none. Strings can never be attached before a fight starts or carried out of one.
engine.cap: 2 (L1–4) · 4 (L5–8) · 5 (L9+) — proficiency bonus, plus 1 from Web of Strings at 5th level
engine.capFormula: your proficiency bonus, plus 1 from Web of Strings at 5th level

triggers.label: I hit with Control Wires — free String

features.name: Strings
features.description: You gain the Strings engine. As a bonus action, you attach a String to a creature you can see within 60 feet (90 at 5th level) — or attach one for free when you hit a creature with your Control Wires. You can maintain up to your String cap (your proficiency bonus) at once. Every other control feature you have keys off a creature you already have a String on; see your Strings engine for how Strings are maintained and lost.
features.narration: A wire goes out from your fingers and finds them, so fine it is mostly invisible until it catches the light. They may not even notice it land. From that moment there is a line between you, and everything you do to them travels down it.
features.sheetSummary: 60 ft (90 at L5). Attach a String to a creature you can see, or for free when you hit with Control Wires. Maintain up to your String cap. Every other control feature requires a String already on the target.

features.name: Strings of Will
features.description: Your art runs on focus and anticipation, not muscle or bluster: you use your Wisdom modifier for attack and damage rolls made with a finesse weapon you're proficient with (your Control Wires, Dagger, or Whip). Any saving throw a Puppeteer feature forces on a creature uses your {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}.
features.narration: You do not overpower anyone. You watch, you wait for the moment the weight shifts, and you pull exactly then — the whole art is knowing which half-second a body cannot correct itself in.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Use your Wisdom modifier for attack and damage rolls with a finesse weapon you're proficient with. Every save a Puppeteer feature forces uses your {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}.

features.name: Bodyguard Strings
features.description: You never meant to take a hit yourself. {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} times per combat, when you are hit by an attack while you have a String attached to another creature within 10 feet of you, you can redirect the attack's damage onto that stringed creature instead of resolving it against you: it takes the full damage of the hit and you take none. Redirecting resolves the attack, so you cannot also Parry the same hit, and it costs you no action or reaction. The wire yanks it into the path — an unwilling creature gets no save; a willing ally may choose to refuse. It works only on a blow with something to step in front of: an attack roll dealing physical or fire damage. It can never take a saving-throw effect, and it can never take psychic damage even from an attack roll — a phantom needle or a suggestion happens inside the target's head, and there is no trajectory to block.
features.narration: The blow is already coming and you do not move. You pull instead, and something else arrives in the space where you were standing — dragged in by the wire, arriving just in time to take what was meant for you.
features.sheetSummary: Free, {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} times per combat. When hit while a String is on another creature within 10 ft, redirect the attack's full damage onto that creature; you take none. Resolves the attack, so you can't also Parry it. No save for an unwilling creature; a willing ally may refuse. Works only on an attack roll dealing physical or fire damage — never a saving-throw effect, never psychic.

features.name: Manipulate
features.description: As an action, choose any number of creatures you currently have a String attached to, each within 60 feet of you. For each one, you pull or push it up to 15 feet in a direction of your choice; this forced movement doesn't provoke opportunity attacks and can drag a creature over or around minor obstacles it could normally cross, but never through solid objects or off a fall it can't survive without consent. An unwilling creature resists: it makes a Strength saving throw against your control DC, and on a success it isn't moved. A willing creature — typically an ally — is simply moved, no save required, letting you yank a friend out of danger or into position exactly as freely as you yank a foe into a wall. Manipulate deals no damage on its own.
features.narration: You lift a hand and they go where you point. Not thrown — walked, dragged, tipped, their own feet betraying them a step at a time while they fight the wire the whole way. An ally you can simply move; an enemy has to be worth the effort.
features.sheetSummary: Any number of Stringed creatures. Pull or push each up to 15 ft; no opportunity attacks provoked. Unwilling: Strength save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}} to resist. Willing: moved automatically. No damage.

meta.save: Str save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}} (unwilling)

features.name: Tricks
features.description: You are a half-caster: your magic is real but it is not the point of you, and it arrives late. From 2nd level you can perform Tricks. You know every trick on the Puppeteer list — a short one — with no preparation and no choosing; each becomes available at the level shown on your class trick ladder, and once available it is always available. Your disciplines are Animation and Legerdemain. Your trick ability is your Wisdom, so your trick save DC is the same number as your Control DC, {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}, and any trick that makes an attack roll uses {{your trick attack|d20 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}. Pledges are at-will and Turns cost you nothing but carry a cooldown in rounds; a Prestige spends Strings and can be performed only once per combat. Casting NEVER generates Strings — that is the full casters' loop, not yours, so a Prestige always comes out of the resource your core kit already needs. A damaging Turn of yours also scales more slowly than a full caster's: see the Tricks and Casting rules page.
features.sheetSummary: Half-caster: tricks from level 2. You know the entire Puppeteer list; each unlocks at its listed level. Disciplines: Animation and Legerdemain. Trick save DC is the same number as your Control DC, {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}; trick attacks use {{your trick attack|d20 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}. Pledges at-will, Turns on cooldown, Prestiges spend Strings and are once per combat. Casting never generates Strings.
features.narration: The wires stop needing to be attached to anything. You work a hand in the empty air and something across the room moves the way a puppet moves, and there is no line anybody can see holding it.

meta.save: Str/Dex/Con/Int/Wis/Cha vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}

features.name: Tangle
features.description: As an action, choose one creature you have a String attached to within 60 feet. If it is unwilling, it must succeed on a Strength saving throw against your control DC or become restrained as wire cinches tight around it; at the end of each of its turns it may repeat the save, ending the restrained condition on a success. If it is willing — an ally you're steadying rather than binding — you instead brace it with your strings, granting it advantage on the next Strength or Dexterity saving throw it makes before the start of your next turn. Measured control: this holds a target in place or steadies a friend, it doesn't end a fight by itself.
features.narration: The wire goes around and then goes tight. It finds elbows, throat, the backs of the knees, and pulls all of them toward each other at once until the thing you caught is a knot standing where it used to be a fighter.
features.sheetSummary: One Stringed creature. Unwilling: Strength save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}} or restrained, repeating the save at the end of each of its turns. Willing: advantage on its next Strength or Dexterity save before the start of your next turn.

meta.save: Str save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}

features.name: Disrupting Pull
features.description: When a creature you have a String attached to makes an attack roll, you can use your reaction to wrench its wire; it must succeed on a Strength saving throw against your control DC or have disadvantage on that attack roll. Alternatively, when a creature you have a String attached to is about to take a reaction (an opportunity attack, for instance), you can use your reaction to yank its string instead; it must succeed on a Strength saving throw against your control DC or that reaction fizzles, accomplishing nothing. Either use spends your one reaction for the round, the same reaction Parry and opportunity attacks draw from — you get one disruption, one Parry, or one opportunity attack per round, never a combination.
features.narration: The swing is halfway out when you twitch two fingers. Something goes wrong in the middle of it — the elbow drops, the shoulder stalls — and the blow that arrives is not the blow that was thrown.
features.sheetSummary: Within leash. When a Stringed creature makes an attack roll, Strength save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}} or it has disadvantage. Or when it is about to take a reaction, Strength save or that reaction fizzles. Uses the same single reaction as Parry.

meta.save: Str save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}

features.name: Guiding Pull
features.description: When a creature you have a String attached to and that is willing to be moved (typically an ally) is targeted by an attack you can see, you can use your reaction to yank it up to 10 feet toward you or to another space within your leash range, before the attack roll is made. If this pulls the target out of the attacker's reach (for a melee attack) or breaks the attacker's line of sight or range (for a ranged attack), the attack automatically misses; otherwise it resolves normally against the target's new position. This draws on the same reaction as Parry, Disrupting Pull, and opportunity attacks — you still get only one reaction per round.
features.narration: You see it coming before your ally does, and you pull. They are yanked half a step sideways with an undignified stumble and the strike closes on empty air behind them, and afterwards they will complain about the bruise on their collarbone.
features.sheetSummary: Before an attack roll against a willing Stringed creature, pull it up to 10 ft toward you or elsewhere in leash. If that puts it out of reach, line of sight, or range, the attack misses automatically. Uses the same single reaction as Parry.

features.name: Grand Marionette
features.description: As an action, choose one hostile creature you have a String attached to within 60 feet. It must make a Strength saving throw against your control DC. On a failure, you seize its body for this turn: you may move it up to its speed (its movement can provoke opportunity attacks as normal) and force it to make a single weapon attack, using its own statistics and weapon, against a target of your choice within its reach or range. Resolve that attack normally, with the creature rolling its own attack and damage. This is your only 'puppet an action' effect at these levels — it grants exactly one forced attack, not a full turn's worth of actions, and the controlled creature otherwise loses the rest of its action and its bonus action for the turn (it keeps its reaction). You can use Grand Marionette once per turn, and only on a creature you already have a String on.
features.narration: You take the whole body. The wires go rigid, the head comes up, and for one horrible moment it walks and strikes exactly as you decide — fighting you the entire time, screaming behind a face that is doing what you told it to.
features.sheetSummary: One hostile Stringed creature. Strength save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}. On a failure, move it up to its speed (provoking as normal) and force one weapon attack with its own statistics against a target you choose. It loses the rest of its action and its bonus action, keeping its reaction.

meta.save: Str save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}

features.name: Web of Strings
features.description: Your control reaches farther and holds more of it at once: your leash range increases from 60 to 90 feet for every String-based feature you have, and your String cap increases by 1 in addition to whatever your proficiency bonus already grants it.
features.narration: Your reach has stopped being a room and started being a stage. The lines run further than anyone can see the end of, and there are more of them than there are people left standing in front of you.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Leash range increases from 60 ft to 90 ft for every String feature. String cap +1 on top of your proficiency bonus.

keyStats.label: Control DC
keyStats.note: Save DC for your String control effects (Manipulate, Tangle, Grand Marionette, etc.). This same number is your trick save DC.

keyStats.label: Strings Cap
keyStats.formula: your proficiency bonus, plus 1 from Web of Strings at 5th level
keyStats.note: Most active Strings you can maintain.

keyStats.label: Parry Base DC
keyStats.note: Worst parrier in the roster; he avoids melee. Lower is better.

classes.name: Sandow
classes.flavor: The circus strongman: feats of raw strength turned into a wall nothing gets past — plant your feet, brace the blow, and throw whatever's left standing.

proficiencies.skills: Choose two from Athletics, Intimidation, Perception, Performance, and Survival

classes.parryReskin: You don't dodge a hit at all — you plant your feet, turn your shoulder or weapon into the line of the blow, and let your frame do what a lesser body couldn't. A Sandow's Parry is a brace, never a step back.
classes.riposte: On a Full Dodge (your Parry d20 roll comes up strictly above your effective Parry DC), the braced impact drives the triggering attacker back: it is pushed 5 feet directly away from you, no save required, at no cost beyond the Parry itself — a shove, not a counterattack. On that same clean brace you may also spend 1 Grit to Brace Up: gain temporary hit points equal to your {{Brace Up|proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}}, lasting until the start of your next turn (like all temporary hit points these don't stack — a new Brace Up replaces any you already have). The shove is free; the Brace Up is the paid option.

engine.name: Grit
engine.description: A pool of raw physical fortitude and adrenaline built from being in the thick of a fight — trading blows, absorbing them, hurling anything not nailed down. The Sandow's sole resource. This baseline generation is shared by every Sandow from 1st level; your Strongman's Act (chosen at 3rd level) layers its own primary Grit stream on top of it — a defensive Act builds more from taking hits, an offensive Act more from dealing them, and Human Cannonball from impacts and forced movement.
engine.generation: Gain 1 Grit the first time each turn you hit a creature with a melee attack, AND gain 1 Grit the first time each turn you are targeted by an attack from any source — whether that attack hits or misses — two separate sources, each capped at once per turn (landing a hit and being attacked in the same turn grants 2 Grit total; further hits you land or attacks made against you that same turn grant no additional Grit from that source). This works from 1st level, before any subclass is chosen.
engine.spend: Spend Grit in 1-point increments to fuel Heave, Brace, and the other feats of strength described in your features. Unspent Grit carries over between rounds, but never between fights: you start every combat with 0 Grit and any left over is lost the moment the fight ends. Grit is a per-combat currency like every other engine in this system — it is built during a fight and cannot be banked before one.

states.label: Iron Grip: holding a creature
states.why: One creature at a time. Crushing or Heaving it ends the hold, and an escapee cannot be re-caught until the end of its next turn.

features.name: Grit
features.description: You gain the Grit pool, a resource built from being in the fray — landing blows and taking them — and spent to fuel your feats of strength. See your Grit engine for exactly how it is generated, spent, and capped.
features.narration: The fight winds you up rather than wearing you down. Every blow you land and every one you take settles into your shoulders as something coiled and useful, and you spend it the way a strongman spends a breath before the lift.
features.sheetSummary: You gain the Grit pool. See the Grit engine for generation, spending, and cap.

features.name: Mighty Build
features.description: You are built on a scale the rules did not plan for. For carrying capacity, and for deciding whether you can grapple, shove, throw or Crush a creature, **you count as one size larger than you actually are** — and you may lay hands on any creature up to that effective size.
features.narration: You are built on the wrong scale for the room. Things that ought to be far too big to shift come off the ground when you decide they will, and the look on their faces is most of the reason you do it. There is a limit. You have met it. It was roughly the size of a barn and it stayed exactly where it was.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Count as one size larger for carrying capacity and for grappling, shoving, throwing or Crushing — and you can handle a creature up to that effective size. See below for what that means at each size; Gargantuan is never available.

meta.uses: Effective size: one step up, Huge maximum

options.group: What you can get hold of
options.name: If you are Medium
options.effect: You count as Large, and can grapple, shove, throw or Crush a creature up to **Large**.

options.group: What you can get hold of
options.name: If you are Large
options.effect: You count as Huge, and can grapple, shove, throw or Crush a creature up to **Huge** — the biggest thing anyone in this game can get their hands on.

options.group: What you can get hold of
options.name: Gargantuan, never
options.effect: Nothing stacks past Huge. Your class caps at Large (see Size on this page), so a Huge target is the ceiling by arithmetic — and it stays the ceiling even if something else were ever to make you larger.

features.name: Iron Grip
features.description: When you hit a creature no larger than Mighty Build allows with a melee attack, you can immediately try to grab it — no extra action or attack, it rides the same hit. The target must succeed on a Strength saving throw against your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}} or be caught: while held it is grappled by you (its speed becomes 0) and has disadvantage on attack rolls it makes against you — pinned against your own frame, its swings at you go wide (its attacks against other creatures are unaffected). The hold has no time limit — the creature does not slip free on its own. It stays grabbed until you cash the hold in by Crushing it (see Crushing Grip) or Heaving it, until you let go or are incapacitated, or until it escapes on its turn by using its action to make a Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics) check against your save DC. When a creature escapes this way it shakes free entirely and can't be caught by your Iron Grip again until the end of its next turn — so you can't chain-grab the same target, though you're free to set your hands on a different one in the meantime. (Ending the hold yourself by Crushing or Heaving the creature does not grant it this reprieve.) You can hold only one creature in your Iron Grip at a time — catching a new target releases the last. A creature held this way counts as grappled by you, so it is a valid target for Heave. Forced movement you cause with your own features (such as a Juggernaut's Bulldozer Charge) never breaks this hold — the creature is dragged with you rather than shoved free.
features.narration: You catch it. Not a hold — a decision — and once your hand closes, the fight it was having with everyone else is over and the fight it is having with you has started. It can swing at you all it likes from there, pressed against your chest with nothing behind the punches.
features.sheetSummary: Free on a melee hit, one creature at a time, reach. Strength save vs your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}} or grappled (speed 0) with disadvantage on attacks against you. No time limit; it ends when you Crush or Heave it, let go, are incapacitated, or it escapes with an action (Athletics or Acrobatics vs {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}}). An escapee can't be re-caught until the end of its next turn. Your own forced movement never breaks the hold.

meta.save: Str save vs {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}}

features.name: Heave
features.description: You grab something heavy — a creature you have grappled, or an object you're holding like a bench, a barrel, or a cage bar — and hurl it. This is used in place of one of your attacks when you take the Attack action (so at 1st level it replaces your single attack; with Extra Attack you can Heave and still swing). Spend 1 to 3 Grit: the thrown target flies 10 feet per point of Grit spent in a direction of your choice and lands in the nearest unoccupied space. What happens on landing depends on the target:
features.narration: You pick it up and you throw it. A man, a bench, a cage bar, a friend who agreed to this — it goes up, it goes out, and it lands somewhere the fight was not expecting a body to land.
features.sheetSummary: In place of one attack, 1-3 Grit. Throw a grappled creature or a held object 10 ft per Grit spent; it lands in the nearest unoccupied space. Landing effects depend on the target.

options.name: Unwilling creature or object
options.effect: A creature you already have grappled (Large or smaller, per Mighty Build), or a heavy object. It takes [[1d6]] bludgeoning damage per point of Grit spent and is knocked prone. No save — you already won the grapple to be holding it, so the throw simply happens.

options.name: Willing ally ("fastball special")
options.effect: No damage and no prone. You place the ally in an unoccupied space within range that has a clear path from you (not through walls or closed doors), ready to act — a launch, not an attack.

features.name: Hold the Line
features.description: When a hostile creature within your reach makes a melee attack against a creature other than you, you can use your reaction to make one melee weapon attack against the attacker. Additionally, whenever a hostile creature within your reach moves in a way that provokes an opportunity attack from you and you hit it with that opportunity attack, its speed becomes 0 for the rest of the current turn — it's stopped where it stands instead of completing its move. Hold the Line draws on the same single reaction as Parry and any other reaction-costed feature you have: punish an attacker or a fleeing creature, or hold your reaction in reserve to Parry — never both on the same round. This is not mind control: a creature is never forced to act against its will, only stopped or made to pay for what it already chose to do.
features.narration: You are standing where you are standing and that is the end of the discussion. Something tries to go past you toward someone smaller, and you make it regret the attempt before it gets there.
features.sheetSummary: Reach. When a hostile in reach melee-attacks someone other than you, make one melee weapon attack against it. Also, when you hit with an opportunity attack, that creature's speed becomes 0 for the rest of its turn. Uses the same single reaction as Parry.

features.name: Brace
features.description: When you take damage from an attack — including one you failed to Parry, or one you had no reaction available to Parry — you can spend Grit, in 1-point increments and at no action cost, to reduce that damage by your {{Brace Soak|2 + your Sandow level}} per point of Grit spent, applied after any Parry multiplier and before the damage is otherwise resolved. The soak climbs with every Sandow level rather than sitting at a flat number that bigger hits quickly outpace, so a point of Grit spent on Brace stays worth it at high levels. Because Brace costs no action or reaction, it stacks with whatever reaction-costed response (or lack of one) you used for the same hit, including a round where your reaction already went to Hold the Line or a Parry. You can spend at most 2 Grit against a single instance of damage, and Brace cannot reduce damage below 0.
features.narration: You see it coming and you set your feet, drop your weight, and take it on the meat of your shoulder. It still hurts. It just does not do what it was supposed to do.
features.sheetSummary: Free, 1-2 Grit per instance of damage. Reduce damage taken by an attack by your {{Brace Soak|2 + your Sandow level}} per Grit spent, applied after any Parry multiplier. Costs no action or reaction, so it stacks with whatever you did with your reaction. Never reduces damage below 0.

features.name: Crushing Grip
features.description: Your hold is a weapon in its own right. While you have a creature caught in your Iron Grip, two things become true. First, the grip turns mobile and sticky: you can drag the held creature with you when you move (it moves with you at no extra cost, staying grappled), and it has disadvantage on any check it makes to escape your grip. Second, you can crush it: in place of one attack when you take the Attack action, spend 1 Grit to deal [[1d6+Str]] bludgeoning damage to the held creature — no attack roll, the grip crushes down and the damage simply lands. You then slam the wrung-out body to the ground: the crushed creature is knocked prone, and the impact ripples outward as a shockwave — each other creature within 5 feet of it must succeed on a Strength saving throw against your save DC or be knocked prone as well. Crushing spends the hold: once you Crush a creature it is no longer grabbed, so to lock it again you must catch it fresh with a new hit. With Extra Attack you can Crush with one attack and make a normal attack with the other to re-catch it (or catch a different target), so a target barely leaves your hands. Unlike Heave, Crushing Grip moves no one — it's a stationary finisher that flattens the held creature and staggers everything pressed in around it.
features.narration: You stop carrying it and start closing your hands. There is no swing to dodge, nothing to parry — just pressure, and then the wrung-out body slammed down flat hard enough that everyone pressed in around it feels the floor jump.
features.sheetSummary: Passive while a creature is in your Iron Grip: drag it with you when you move at no extra cost, and it has disadvantage on escape checks. In place of one attack, 1 Grit: deal [[1d6+Str]] bludgeoning to the held creature with no attack roll, knock it prone, and each other creature within 5 ft makes a Strength save vs {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}} or is knocked prone. Crushing releases the hold.

meta.save: Str save vs your DC (shockwave, nearby creatures)

features.name: Extra Attack
features.description: You can attack twice, instead of once, whenever you take the Attack action on your turn.
features.narration: One swing was never really your rhythm. You work in pairs now, the second already loading while the first lands.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Attack twice instead of once when you take the Attack action.

features.name: Earthshaker
features.description: As an action, spend 3 Grit to slam a weapon, fist, or heavy object into the ground and send a shockwave through every creature of your choice within 15 feet of you. Each must succeed on a Strength saving throw against your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}} or be pushed 5 feet directly away from you and knocked prone. Earthshaker deals no damage on its own — it's forced movement and control, a battlefield reset, not another source of hurt. You can use Earthshaker once per turn.
features.narration: You bring everything you have down into the floor. The boards jump, the dust comes off the rafters, and everyone standing near you discovers they are no longer standing.
features.sheetSummary: 15-ft radius, creatures of your choice. Strength save vs your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}} or pushed 5 ft away from you and knocked prone. No damage.

meta.save: Str save vs {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}}

keyStats.note: Save DC for effects your features force (e.g. Heave, Earthshaker).

keyStats.label: Grit Cap
keyStats.note: Most Grit you can hold at once.

keyStats.label: Brace Soak
keyStats.formula: 2 + your Sandow level, per point of Grit spent (max 2 Grit)
keyStats.note: Damage Brace removes, after any Parry multiplier.

keyStats.label: Parry Base DC
keyStats.note: Second-best parrier; lower is better.

subclasses.name: Anarchist
subclasses.flavor: The demolition act of the deck: a Joker who trades sleight of hand for lit fuses, packing his cards with flash powder and treating the whole crowd, friend or foe, as fair game for the blast radius.

features.name: Powder Burst
features.description: As an action, spend 2 Mayhem to hurl a spray of flash-powder cards that detonate in a 10-foot-radius sphere centered on a point you can see within 60 feet. Each creature in that area must make a Dexterity saving throw against your gambit DC, taking [[2d6]] fire damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one. You can use Powder Burst only once per turn, and only when you have Mayhem to spend on it — it draws on the same small pool as everything else you do, so it is bounded by how much chaos you've actually generated this fight, not something you can chain turn after turn.
features.narration: You throw a fistful of cards and they go up mid-air — a white crack of flash-powder and heat where the fan opened. For a second afterwards the whole room is negative-coloured and nobody is looking at you, which was rather the idea.
features.sheetSummary: 10-ft radius within 60 ft. Dexterity save vs {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}}. Fail: [[2d6]] fire. Success: half damage.

meta.save: Dex save vs {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}}

features.name: Collateral Chaos
features.description: Your chaos never stays contained to one target. The first time each turn you resolve a Wild Card result or a Gambit option that targets a single creature, and a second valid target for that same effect (an additional hostile creature if the original target was hostile, or an additional willing ally if the original was an ally) is within 5 feet of the original target, you may extend the effect to that second creature as well. The second creature is affected exactly as the first, including making its own saving throw if the effect calls for one. This costs no additional Mayhem, happens as part of the Wild Card or Gambit you're already resolving (not a separate action or reaction), and can happen only once per turn.
features.narration: Whatever you did to one of them does not have the manners to stop there. It splashes — the same joke, the same trick, the same unpleasant surprise landing on whoever had the poor judgement to be standing next to them.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. The first time each turn a Wild Card or Gambit targets a single creature, extend it to one more valid target of the same kind within 5 ft of the original. The second creature makes its own save. Costs no extra Mayhem and no action.

features.name: Demolitionist's Eye
features.description: You read a building the way a card sharp reads a table: where it's weak, where it's load-bearing, and exactly what a charge in the wrong pocket would do to it. By studying a structure, wall, door, or large object for 1 minute, you learn its weak points, what it would take to bring it down, and how it would fall. You have advantage on ability checks made to break, breach, or dismantle objects and structures, and your damage against objects and structures is doubled. You can also pop a harmless flash or bang from a treated card at any point you can see within 60 feet — a distraction, a signal, or a very convincing bluff.
features.narration: You look at a wall the way a card sharp looks at a table. The load-bearing beam, the tired mortar, the door that only pretends to be solid — you can see the whole ugly skeleton of a building and exactly where to hit it to make it stop being one.
features.sheetSummary: Study a structure/object 1 min: learn its weak points. Advantage on checks to break/breach objects; double damage vs objects and structures. Pop a harmless flash-bang at a point within 60 ft.

subclasses.name: Buffoon
subclasses.flavor: The bit is that you will not stop. They hit you, you get up, you make the joke again. Eventually it stops being funny for them. The Buffoon is the Jester who keeps the company upright — the only source of true healing anywhere in the circus.

features.name: Take the Fall
features.description: When an attack **hits** an ally within 10 feet of you, you can use your reaction to get in the way. This resolves after the attack has already hit: **nothing is re-rolled and your own AC never comes into it** — the blow was always going to land, and you are only deciding who it lands on. You take the damage in your ally's place, and you take **half** of it. Because your reaction is spent doing this, you cannot Parry the same blow, and this never counts as a Parry.
features.sheetSummary: When an attack hits an ally you take it instead, at HALF damage. Its requirements and how it resolves are listed below.
features.narration: You do not push anybody. You could not shift the strongman if you tried, and you have never once got there in time. What you do is trip — a beautifully judged, entirely deliberate accident that puts you in the path with your feet already going out from under you. The blow catches you on the way down instead of square on, and you ride it into the floor, roll through it, and come up talking. It is the oldest thing you know how to do: you have been falling over professionally since you were nine, and the whole craft of it is that the floor never gets you as hard as it should.

options.name: You must see the attacker
options.effect: You cannot intercept a blow you never saw coming.

options.name: Something physical only
options.effect: An attack roll dealing physical or fire damage. Never a saving-throw effect, and never psychic damage even from an attack roll — there is no trajectory to step into.

options.name: The hit has already landed
options.effect: You do not re-roll the attack and it is not compared to your AC. The damage is rolled once and you take half of it, rounded down; your ally takes none.

options.name: It costs your reaction
options.effect: You cannot also Parry that blow, and this never counts as a Parry. Any damage reduction you have applies to your half as normal.

features.name: Rubber Bones
features.description: You have been thrown off more stages than you can count. You have resistance to bludgeoning damage from falls, collisions, and being thrown, and whenever you are knocked prone you can stand up for 5 feet of movement instead of half your speed.
features.sheetSummary: Resistance to bludgeoning damage from falls, collisions, and being thrown. Standing up from prone costs 5 ft of movement instead of half your speed.
features.narration: Same trick, all the time, whether anybody threw anything or not. You go down the way a dropped coat goes down — loose, folding, nothing locked — and the ground takes almost nothing off you. Getting back up is the easy half; you have never once had to think about it.

features.name: Beneath Contempt
features.description: Nobody guards their tongue in front of the fool. Guards, servants, courtiers, and hired muscle routinely discuss things in front of you that they would never say to an armed stranger, and you have advantage on Charisma (Deception) checks made to be dismissed as harmless. A creature that has already seen you do something dangerous is immune to this for as long as it remembers.
features.sheetSummary: Guards, servants and hired muscle speak freely in front of you. Advantage on Charisma (Deception) checks made to be dismissed as harmless. A creature that has seen you do something dangerous is immune to this for as long as it remembers.
features.narration: They look straight through you and carry on the conversation. You are furniture that occasionally makes a noise, and you have built an entire career out of what people say in front of furniture.

subclasses.name: Bulwark
subclasses.flavor: The tank's discipline: a Sandow who plants himself between the crowd and the danger and simply refuses to move, soaking up every blow the show throws at him and daring anything to get past.

features.name: Iron Resolve
features.description: Your body is trained to feed off danger, your own and the danger aimed at those you're shielding. In addition to your baseline Grit generation, you gain 1 additional Grit the first time each turn you are targeted by an attack from any source (whether it hits or misses), and you gain 1 Grit the first time each turn a hostile creature targets an ally within 5 feet of you with an attack (attacks against you are already covered by the first clause) — two separate sources, each capped at once per turn, exactly like your baseline Grit generation. Standing at the front and drawing fire, onto himself or off an ally, is how a Bulwark keeps his Grit topped up.
features.narration: Being shot at agrees with you. Every blade that turns your way, every arrow meant for the smaller person behind you, settles in your chest as something hot and useful — you are never so full of fight as when the whole room is trying to get through you.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. On top of baseline Grit: +1 Grit the first time each turn you are targeted by an attack (hit or miss), and +1 Grit the first time each turn a hostile targets an ally within 5 ft of you. Two sources, each once per turn.

features.name: Guardian's Wall
features.description: You make yourself the obstacle nothing gets past. Its protection works three ways:
features.narration: You plant yourself and become architecture. People who wanted to go somewhere discover that the somewhere is behind you, and the blow aimed past your shoulder finds your shoulder instead because you put it there.
features.sheetSummary: Passive and free. Three separate protections, listed in the table below: a 10-ft taunt, an intercept usable once per turn on an ally within 5 ft, and the wall's standing benefit.

options.name: Challenge (taunt)
options.effect: While you have at least 1 Grit, every enemy within 10 feet of you has disadvantage on any attack roll that does not include you as a target — swing at your allies and your bulk is always in the line. An enemy can still act freely by targeting you instead, or by stepping out of your 10-foot reach.

options.name: Intercept
options.effect: Once per turn, when a creature you can see within 5 feet of you is hit by an attack, you can throw yourself into the blow — the attack's damage is dealt to you instead of the original target. This costs you nothing and does not use your reaction, so it never competes with Parry or Hold the Line. You may reduce the damage with Brace as normal, but you cannot Parry a hit you Intercept — it has already landed. It works only on a blow with something to step in front of: an attack roll dealing physical or fire damage. It can never take a saving-throw effect, and it can never take psychic damage even from an attack roll — a phantom needle or a suggestion happens inside the target's head, and there is no trajectory to block.

options.name: Braced Footing
options.effect: While you have at least 1 Grit, you have advantage on saving throws to avoid being knocked prone or forcibly moved.

features.name: Living Barricade
features.description: You are a wall that walks, and everyone who has ever tried to get past you knows it. Outside combat, you count as one size larger and have advantage on any check made to block a passage, hold a door or gate shut, anchor a rope or a person, or resist being moved or dragged. A doorway, corridor, or gap you choose to fill with your body cannot be squeezed past without your permission.
features.narration: Doors do not close on their own when you are leaning on them, and corridors stop being corridors. You have held a gate against a mob before, and the memory of it is written on the faces of everyone who tries you a second time.
features.sheetSummary: Count as one size larger + advantage on checks to block passages, hold doors shut, anchor ropes/people, or resist being moved. A gap you fill can't be squeezed past without your consent.

subclasses.name: Contortionist
subclasses.flavor: The escape artist's discipline: a body trained to fold, slip, and pour itself through gaps that were never meant to admit a person, and to shrug off every rope, cage, or grip a captor thinks is secure.

features.name: Contortion
features.description: You gain a pool of Contortion Dice (d6) each combat: {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} of them, refilling at the start of every fight. When a creature you can see hits you with an attack, before you decide whether to Parry, you can spend one Contortion Die — this costs no reaction and no action — and roll it. On a 4 or higher you fold your body around the strike: you take no damage from the attack, the attacker takes half of the damage it would have dealt you (rounded down, of the same type), and your reaction stays free. On a 3 or lower the fold fails and the die is spent — the hit is not turned aside, but you may still spend your reaction to Parry it as normal if you have a reaction available; if your reaction is already gone, the attack lands in full. Because Contortion is not itself a Parry, a successful fold does not trigger Counterflow, Flowing Reflexes, or Riposte, and it sits in front of your Parry as an extra, die-gated chance to avoid a hit.
features.narration: The strike arrives and your body simply is not shaped that way any more. You fold around the blade — spine, ribs, shoulder all going somewhere they should not go — and the blow slides through the space where a person used to be, its own force wrenching back against the arm that threw it.
features.sheetSummary: When hit, before deciding whether to Parry. {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} Contortion Dice (d6) per combat, costing no action or reaction. Roll one: on a 4+ you take no damage, the attacker takes half the damage it would have dealt (same type), and your reaction stays free. On a 3 or lower the die is spent and you may still Parry.
