Not a Parry, so it never triggers Counterflow, Flowing Reflexes, or Riposte.

features.name: Reversal
features.description: A successful contortion doesn't just save you — it wrong-foots your attacker. Immediately after your Contortion succeeds (you roll 4 or higher on a Contortion Die and fold a hit away), you may move up to 10 feet without provoking opportunity attacks, and the next attack roll you make before the end of your next turn has advantage. The attacker overcommitted on a blow that found only empty air, and you take the opening. From 5th level, a failed defence has an answer too: when a creature within 5 feet of you hits you — the moment your Contortion fold and your Parry have both failed and the blow has actually landed — you can use your reaction to pour your body along the line of the strike and snap back from an angle it can't cover. Make one melee weapon attack against that creature; on a hit, you immediately flow up to 10 feet without provoking opportunity attacks, leaving it striking at the space you just left. This draws on the same single reaction as Parry, so on most rounds it is the counter you take when your defence has already failed you; on a turn when Flowing Reflexes (3rd level) hands your reaction back after a clean Parry, it becomes a second, offensive use of that same reaction against the next foe to land a hit. The reactive slip is off-turn movement and generates no Momentum.
features.narration: Coming out of the fold you are already moving, and they are still leaning into a swing that found nothing. You take the gap. And on the occasions the fold fails and the blade truly lands, you pour yourself along it anyway and come back from an angle no guard covers.
features.sheetSummary: After a successful Contortion, move up to 10 ft without provoking and your next attack roll before the end of your next turn has advantage. From 5th level, when a creature within 5 ft hits you after both your Contortion and Parry have failed, use your reaction to make one melee weapon attack against it; on a hit, move up to 10 ft without provoking. Uses the same single reaction as Parry; generates no Momentum.

features.name: Sideshow Escapist
features.description: Your act is escape itself, and no lock, rope, or cage in the show has ever held you through a full performance. You can squeeze through any gap wide enough for your head, moving at half speed while you do. Given 1 minute of wriggling, you automatically escape any nonmagical restraint — ropes, chains, manacles, a straitjacket, a locked stock. You also have advantage on Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) and Dexterity (Acrobatics) checks made to slip bonds discreetly or to hide in cramped spaces a person shouldn't fit.
features.narration: Nothing built has ever held you for a full performance. You go through gaps no shoulders should fit, and given a minute alone with a rope, a chain, or a locked stock, you simply are not in it any more.
features.sheetSummary: Squeeze through any head-sized gap at half speed. Escape any nonmagical restraint automatically in 1 minute. Advantage on checks to slip bonds discreetly or hide in cramped spaces.

subclasses.name: Fatemonger
subclasses.flavor: Luck is a resource like any other. It belongs to whoever is paying attention, and nobody in this company pays attention like you. The Fatemonger is the Jester who makes misfortune land on someone — the damage discipline of a class that otherwise buffs and mends.

features.name: Loaded Odds
features.description: You do not let a bad roll stand. When an ally you can see within 30 feet rolls a 1 on a d20 for an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw, you can make them reroll it for free — no action, once on each of your turns. Separately, once on each of your turns you can spend 1 Mirth to make an ally within 30 feet reroll ANY d20 they just rolled, whatever the number was. Either way they must use the new result.
features.sheetSummary: Free, 1/turn: an ally who rolls a 1 on a d20 rerolls it. Also 1/turn, for 1 Mirth: an ally rerolls ANY d20 they just rolled. They must use the new result.
features.narration: You tut, or click your tongue, or simply look at them — and the moment gets a second go at itself. Nobody has ever been able to explain how you do it, least of all you.

features.name: The House Always Collects
features.description: Fortune runs both ways at your table, and you take a cut of every swing of it. You gain 1 Mirth whenever a creature you can see within 30 feet rolls a natural 20 or a natural 1 on an attack roll — the disaster and the miracle are both material, and you were watching either way.
features.sheetSummary: Gain 1 Mirth whenever a creature you can see within 30 ft rolls a natural 20 or a natural 1 on an attack roll.
features.narration: The worst possible thing happens and you laugh first, because a disaster is just a setup with better timing, and you have already worked out what it is setting up.

features.name: Never Pays to Bet Against Him
features.description: You have an unnatural nose for a wager. You know instinctively whether a game of chance, a contract, or an offer put to you is rigged, though not how. When you make a bet, a bargain, or a wager of any kind and lose, you may declare that you meant to — you recover whatever you staked, and everyone present remembers it as a joke you were making.
features.sheetSummary: You instinctively know whether a game, contract, or offer is rigged, but not how. When you lose a bet or bargain, declare you meant to: you recover your stake and everyone remembers it as a joke. The same crowd never falls for it twice.
features.narration: You lose spectacularly, take a bow for it, and by the time the laugh dies down the money is back in your hand and nobody can reconstruct how the bet was ever serious.

meta.uses: No limit; the same crowd only once

subclasses.name: Firebrand
subclasses.flavor: The fire act: a juggler whose cascade is a ring of burning orbs, trading the clean kill for spreading flame and scorched ground nobody wants to cross.

features.name: Ignite
features.description: Your implements trail fire. A creature hit by at least one of your implements on your turn is set alight and takes [[1d4]] fire damage at the start of its next turn — this is added on top of the implement's normal damage, not a replacement for it, and the die scales as your implements do. The flames flare at the start of the creature's turn and then gutter out, so there is no window for it to smother them first; hit it again and it simply burns again the following turn.
features.narration: Everything that leaves your hands is trailing flame. It catches on whatever it touches, and a moment later the thing you hit remembers it is burning, usually at the worst possible point in its own swing.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. A creature hit by at least one implement on your turn takes [[1d4]] fire damage at the start of its next turn, on top of the implement's normal damage.

features.name: Wildfire
features.description: Once on each of your turns, one implement you throw can burst on impact instead of ricocheting: each creature within 10 feet of the space it strikes must make a Dexterity saving throw against your {{Trick Shot DC|6 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}}, taking [[2d4]] fire damage on a failure or half as much on a success. That space then burns until the start of your next turn — the first time a creature enters it on a turn, or ends its turn there, it takes [[1d4]] fire damage.
features.narration: One of them does not carom off — it bursts, a low orange bloom that goes out sideways and leaves the floor burning behind it. That patch stays lit and stays angry, and anyone who wants to cross it is going to have opinions about it afterwards.
features.sheetSummary: Part of your Barrage, 10-ft burst. One implement bursts instead of ricocheting: Dexterity save vs your {{Trick Shot DC|6 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}}, [[2d4]] fire on a failure, half on a success. That space burns until the start of your next turn, dealing [[1d4]] fire the first time a creature enters it on a turn or ends its turn there.

meta.save: Dex vs Trick Shot DC

features.name: Fire-Eater's Trade
features.description: Before the fire was a weapon, it was the act. You can eat, breathe, and dance with flame harmlessly for a crowd. You can light or snuff any mundane flame you can see within 30 feet — a candle, a torch, a campfire — at will, no action required on your turn. Ordinary open flames can't harm you (fire damage from attacks, spells, and hazards still can), your implements can burn as torches without being consumed, and you have advantage on Charisma (Performance) checks that use fire.
features.narration: Before it was a weapon it was the finale: flame swallowed, flame breathed, flame walked along your knuckles for a paying crowd. Fire is a colleague, not a hazard, and every candle in the room answers you.
features.sheetSummary: Light/snuff any mundane flame within 30 ft at will. Ordinary open flames can't harm you (fire damage from attacks/spells/hazards still can). Implements burn as torches unconsumed. Advantage on fire Performance checks.

subclasses.name: Gambler
subclasses.flavor: The card-sharp's discipline: a Joker who trusts the deck more than his own hands, having learned exactly which rolls can be nudged in his favor, which bets are worth doubling, and which are strictly for suckers.

features.name: Stacked Deck
features.description: You've learned to load the deck in your favor. {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} times per combat, you can do one of the following, no action required: choose the result of a Wild Card draw instead of rolling the d8; reroll a d20 you just rolled for your own attack roll, ability check, or saving throw and use the new result; or target one creature within 30 feet of you that just made an attack roll or saving throw, forcing it to succeed on a Charisma saving throw against your gambit DC or reroll that d20 and use the new result. These uses cost no Mayhem and draw on nothing else you have.
features.narration: The deck was never honest and neither were you. When the moment matters you simply arrange for the result you needed — or reach across the table and make somebody else take theirs again, which is worse.
features.sheetSummary: Free, {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} times per combat. Choose one: pick a Wild Card result instead of rolling; reroll your own d20 attack, check, or save and use the new result; or force a creature that just rolled a d20 to make a Charisma save vs {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}} or reroll and use the new result. Costs no Mayhem.

meta.save: Cha save vs {{gambit DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Charisma modifier}} (forced reroll)

features.name: Double Down
features.description: You can bet on your own luck before you know how a roll lands. Once per turn, before making an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw (not a Parry roll), you can spend 1 Mayhem to roll a d6 and add it to the total. If that d6 comes up a 1, the bet turns on you: you take [[1d4]] psychic damage as the trick backfires, in addition to whatever the roll itself produces. You must decide to Double Down before the roll's outcome is known.
features.narration: You commit before you know. The bet goes down while the outcome is still in the air, and most of the time it comes back better than it had any right to. Occasionally it turns on you, and the recoil of it hurts somewhere behind your eyes.
features.sheetSummary: Free, declared before the roll. Add a d6 to an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw (never a Parry). If the d6 comes up 1, you take [[1d4]] psychic damage.

features.name: Card Sharp
features.description: You've sat at every kind of table and walked away from all of them ahead. By handling the pieces, you instantly recognize loaded dice, marked cards, or any rigged game of chance. In games of chance or gambling skill against nonmagical opposition you have advantage on any check involved, and you can cheat without being caught by anything short of magic (opposed Sleight of Hand checks made to cheat are rolled with advantage). You also have advantage on Wisdom (Insight) checks to tell whether someone is bluffing about a bet, a deal, or a debt.
features.narration: You have sat at every kind of crooked table there is and walked away from all of them ahead. Loaded dice announce themselves in your palm, marked cards feel wrong on the shuffle, and nobody has ever caught you doing what you are doing.
features.sheetSummary: Auto-detect rigged games by handling them. Advantage on game-of-chance checks and on cheating undetected (vs nonmagical opposition). Advantage on Insight vs bluffs in bets, deals, and debts.

subclasses.name: Harlequin
subclasses.flavor: The maddest act under the big top: a Joker who stops treating melee as something to avoid and starts treating a ring full of enemies as the best possible stage, grinning wider the closer the danger gets.

features.name: Reckless Grin
features.description: As a bonus action, spend 1 Mayhem to throw caution to the wind until the start of your next turn: you have advantage on melee attack rolls you make with a finesse weapon you're proficient with, but attack rolls against you also have advantage until the start of your next turn. You can only be under the effect of Reckless Grin once at a time; using it again while it is already active changes nothing and doesn't cost additional Mayhem.
features.narration: You stop defending. The grin arrives first and then you do, swinging into range with your guard nowhere at all, and for a few glorious seconds you are hitting a great deal harder than anybody hitting you can quite believe — and they are all hitting you.
features.sheetSummary: Until the start of your next turn you have advantage on melee attacks with a finesse weapon you're proficient with, and attack rolls against you have advantage. Doesn't stack with itself.

features.name: Center of the Ring
features.description: You thrive surrounded by danger. At the start of your turn, if you are within 5 feet of at least two hostile creatures, you gain temporary hit points equal to your {{Charisma modifier (min 1)|set from your stats on your character sheet}}, and for the rest of the turn moving through a space occupied by a hostile creature costs you no extra movement (you still can't end your movement there). As with temporary hit points from any other source, these don't stack — if you already have some, keep whichever total is higher.
features.narration: You are happiest with the ring closed around you. Surrounded, outnumbered, laughing — something in you sits up and starts working, and you slip between them like they are scenery rather than people.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. At the start of your turn, if at least two hostiles are within 5 ft, gain temporary hit points equal to your {{Charisma modifier (min 1)|set from your stats on your character sheet}}, and for that turn moving through a hostile's space costs no extra movement. Temporary hit points don't stack.

features.name: Jester's License
features.description: The fool may say what the courtier cannot. When you frame it as performance — a jest, a song, a pantomime — you can deliver insults, accusations, and uncomfortable truths without your audience turning violent: creatures may eject you, despise you, or plot quietly, but they don't move to harm you for the words alone. You also have advantage on Charisma (Performance) checks, and on Charisma (Persuasion) checks made while playing the fool.
features.narration: The fool says what the courtier cannot. Wrap it in a song, a jest, a bit of pantomime, and the truth goes down where a plain sentence would have got you killed — they may loathe you, they may throw you out, but they laugh first.
features.sheetSummary: Insults/accusations/hard truths delivered as performance don't provoke violence (targets may still eject or resent you). Advantage on Performance checks and on Persuasion while playing the fool.

subclasses.name: Human Cannonball
subclasses.flavor: The mobility discipline: a Sandow who treats his own body as the act's headline stunt, hurling himself across the ring as a living projectile and slamming into whatever, or whoever, is waiting on the other side.

features.name: Kinetic Buildup
features.description: You build charge the way a cannon builds pressure, through speed and impact. In addition to your baseline Grit generation, you gain 1 additional Grit the first time each turn you move at least half your speed in a straight line and then hit a creature with a melee attack before the end of that turn, and you gain 1 Grit the first time each turn a creature takes damage from your Cannon Launch — the impact of a landing slam feeding your next charge. Two separate sources, each capped at once per turn, exactly like your baseline Grit generation.
features.narration: You run on pressure. A straight sprint into something solid does for you what a long rest does for other people, and every landing packs the next launch tighter.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. On top of baseline Grit: +1 Grit the first time each turn you move at least half your speed in a straight line and then hit with a melee attack, and +1 Grit the first time each turn a creature takes damage from your Cannon Launch. Two sources, each once per turn.

features.name: Cannon Launch
features.description: As a bonus action, spend 2 Grit to launch yourself up to 30 feet in a straight line to an unoccupied space you can see. This movement doesn't provoke opportunity attacks and never causes fall damage from the arc, however dramatic it looks. If you end that movement within 5 feet of a hostile creature, or pass through a hostile creature's space en route (stopping in the nearest available space when you do), that creature must succeed on a Strength saving throw against your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}} or take [[2d6]] bludgeoning damage and be knocked prone. You can use Cannon Launch only once per turn. Additionally, when you use Heave's fastball special to throw a willing ally, the throw's range increases to 20 feet per point of Grit spent, instead of the normal 10.
features.narration: You go off like the cannon you are named for — a flat, absurd arc across the room ending in whoever was unlucky enough to be under it. There is no landing technique. There is only arrival.
features.sheetSummary: Launch in a straight line to a space you can see; no opportunity attacks and no fall damage. A hostile you end within 5 ft of, or pass through, makes a Strength save vs your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}} or takes [[2d6]] bludgeoning and is knocked prone. Also raises Heave's fastball special to 20 ft per Grit.

meta.save: Str save vs {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}}

features.name: Death-Defying Stunt
features.description: Launching yourself at things is not just a combat trick — it's the act. Your long jump distance is doubled and your high jump increases by 10 feet. You land any deliberate jump or drop of 30 feet or less on your feet, unharmed and looking spectacular. You also have advantage on Charisma (Performance) and Dexterity (Acrobatics) checks made as part of a stunt.
features.narration: Distance stopped being an obstacle for you a long time ago. You leap what should not be leapt, drop what should not be dropped, and land on your feet with your arms out, waiting for applause that does not always come.
features.sheetSummary: Long jump doubled; high jump +10 ft. Land any deliberate jump/drop of 30 ft or less unharmed. Advantage on Performance and Acrobatics checks made as part of a stunt.

subclasses.name: Hypnotist
subclasses.flavor: You do not need them to see anything. You need them to agree with you, and people agree with far more than they think they do. The Hypnotist is the Illusionist who works on the mind directly — and the only one who adds tricks to his own list.

features.name: Suggestion Under the Patter
features.description: You never stop talking, and none of it sounds like an order. Once on each of your turns, as a bonus action, choose one creature within 30 feet that can hear and understand you. It must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw against your {{trick save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}} or, on its next turn, it cannot willingly move closer to you and cannot target you with an attack. It may act freely otherwise — this never takes its turn away, it only takes YOU off the list of things it is willing to do something about. This costs nothing and has no daily limit: keeping one creature off you is simply what a Hypnotist does with his bonus action.
features.sheetSummary: No cost. Target must hear and understand you. Wisdom save vs {{trick save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}} or on its next turn it can't willingly move closer to you and can't target you with an attack. It acts freely otherwise.
features.narration: You keep talking. Nothing you say is an order and none of it sounds like magic, and somewhere in the middle of it the thing decides, entirely on its own, that you are not who it wants to be dealing with.

meta.save: Wis save vs {{trick save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}}

features.name: Sympathetic Response
features.description: This discipline adds two Mesmerism tricks to your list, free and permanent: **Lull** (level 2) and **The Suggestion** (level 3). They are yours alone — no other Illusionist learns them — and they are what this feature is built on, because the base Illusionist list carries almost no Mesmerism at all. On top of that, a mind you have opened stays open: when a creature fails a saving throw against one of your Mesmerism tricks, it has **disadvantage on every attack roll and every saving throw it makes until the end of its next turn**. It is not helpless and nobody gets a free shot at it — it is simply worse at all of it, for a while, because part of it is still listening to you.
features.sheetSummary: When a creature fails a save against one of your Mesmerism tricks, it has disadvantage on every attack roll and saving throw it makes until the end of its next turn.
features.narration: You open something in them and it stays open. Their swings come in half-committed and their mind will not close around anything, because part of it is still back in the room with your voice.

features.name: Stage Hypnosis
features.description: The old parlour act still works. Over 1 minute of uninterrupted talk with a willing or unsuspecting creature that can hear and understand you, you can put it into a light trance. While entranced it is calm, suggestible, and answers questions truthfully as it understands them, and it remembers the conversation afterwards as pleasant and unremarkable. The trance ends instantly if it is harmed, threatened, or asked to do something it would refuse while awake. This does no combat work and never functions on a creature already hostile to you.
features.sheetSummary: 1 minute of uninterrupted talk with a willing or unsuspecting creature that can hear and understand you: it enters a light trance, answers truthfully as it understands things, and remembers the talk as unremarkable. Ends if harmed, threatened, or asked to do something it would refuse. Never works on an already-hostile creature; no combat use.
features.narration: Watch the coin. Listen to the voice. There is nothing frightening about any of it — that is the whole craft — and ten minutes later they walk away pleased with a conversation they cannot quite recount.

subclasses.name: Impalement
subclasses.flavor: The impalement act: a juggler who doesn't spray steel but places it — one studied target, every blade finding the same fatal seam.

features.name: Mark
features.description: As a bonus action, you can Mark one creature you can see — a cold read of its guard and rhythm. Until the end of your next turn, your thrown implements score a critical hit against the Marked creature on a roll of 19 or 20, and the first of your implements to hit it each turn deals extra damage equal to your {{Intelligence modifier|set from your stats on your character sheet}}. You can have only one creature Marked at a time; Marking a new one ends the old.
features.narration: You watch one of them for a moment — the guard, the rhythm, the tell in the shoulder before it commits. After that you are not really aiming any more; you are just waiting for the gap you already know is coming.
features.sheetSummary: One creature at a time, within sight. Until the end of your next turn your thrown implements crit against it on a 19 or 20, and your first implement to hit it each turn deals extra damage equal to your {{Intelligence modifier|set from your stats on your character sheet}}.

features.name: Impossible Shot
features.description: Your calculations beat the battlefield. Your thrown implements ignore half and three-quarters cover, and they suffer no disadvantage anywhere within their full range: a normal throw reaches 20 feet, and you simply ignore the long-range penalty that would otherwise apply on throws from 20 out to 60 feet. Every angle is a clean angle.
features.narration: Cover is a suggestion. You throw through gaps that were not gaps a moment ago, off angles that should not connect, at ranges where anyone else would be guessing, and it all lands as though the room had been arranged for it.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Your thrown implements ignore half and three-quarters cover and take no long-range disadvantage anywhere within their full 60-ft range.

features.name: Sideshow Precision
features.description: You have split apples on volunteers' heads for years, and you have never once hit the volunteer. Your thrown implements automatically hit any stationary object target you can see within range — no roll needed. You can pin a willing or unaware creature's clothing to a nearby surface with a throw, holding it in place until it spends an action tearing free. You never hit an unintended creature with a thrown implement, and you have advantage on Charisma (Performance) checks built around throwing.
features.narration: Years of splitting apples on volunteers' heads, and never once the volunteer. You can pin a sleeve to a post without touching the arm inside it, and everyone who has ever stood against your board knows exactly how steady your hand is.
features.sheetSummary: Thrown implements auto-hit stationary objects in range. Pin a willing/unaware creature's clothing to a surface (it spends an action to tear free). Never hit bystanders by accident. Advantage on throwing-act Performance checks.

subclasses.name: Impersonator
subclasses.flavor: The discipline of the mimic: a Doppelganger who spends less time studying combat forms and more time studying people — their faces, their voices, their little tells — until borrowing a life, or a single trick from one, is second nature.

features.name: Perfect Mimicry
features.description: You have practiced copying more than a silhouette. As an action, you can assume the exact physical appearance — clothing, minor scars, voice, and posture included — of any Medium or Small humanoid you have observed for at least 1 minute, for up to 1 hour or until you end it early (no action required) or use this feature again. This changes only your outward appearance, not your game statistics, and any equipment you're wearing or carrying isn't transformed along with you. While disguised this way, you have advantage on Charisma (Deception) checks made to pass yourself off as that specific individual, and a creature without a particular reason to be suspicious can't tell you're a fake without succeeding on a Wisdom (Insight) check contested by your Deception check (or other means, such as true seeing). There is no limit on how often you do this — you hold **one** face at a time, and taking a new one ends the old.
features.narration: You put on a face like a coat. Not a disguise — the scar, the voice, the way they stand when they are bored, all of it, down to the habits they do not know they have. People who have known them for years walk straight past you.

meta.uses: At will, one at a time

features.sheetSummary: At will, 1 hour, one face at a time. Assume the exact appearance and voice of a Medium or Small humanoid you observed for 1+ minute. Appearance only — statistics and gear are unchanged. Advantage on Deception to pass as them; seeing through it takes an Insight check vs your Deception.

features.name: Borrowed Trick
features.description:
You do not copy what a blow was made of — you copy the thing that made it. When a creature you can see within 30 feet makes an attack, hit or miss, you memorise that attack. You hold one at a time; memorising a new one replaces it, and it fades when the fight ends.

**Once per combat, the next Clone you create comes out as a Mimic** — it wears that creature's face and build instead of yours. In every other respect it is an ordinary Clone: it counts against your cap, obeys your leash, and can be used by Swap, Mirror Image, Decoy Detonation and the rest.
features.narration: You watch it swing once and that is all you need. The next reflection you leave behind is not wearing your face — it is wearing theirs, standing where you put it, holding the same weapon at the same angle. The look on the original's face is the entire reason you learned this.
features.sheetSummary: Memorise an attack made by a creature you can see within 30 ft (hit or miss); you hold one at a time. Once per combat, your next Clone spawns as a Mimic of that creature. What it copies and its limits are listed below.

meta.action: Free to memorise · Bonus Action to create

options.name: Its face and build
options.effect: The Clone looks like the memorised creature rather than like you.

options.name: Its Armour Class
options.effect: The Mimic uses the copied creature's AC instead of yours — which can be better or worse than your own.

options.name: That one attack, and nothing else
options.effect: Whenever the Mimic attacks — through Mirror Barrage, Mirror Assault, or any feature that has a Clone strike — it makes the memorised attack, using the copied creature's attack bonus and damage, instead of your weapon and Constitution. It has no other action, trait or ability of that creature.

options.name: Nothing bigger than you
options.effect: You can only mimic a creature of your own size or smaller. A Medium Doppelganger can copy a Small or Medium creature and can never copy a Large or Huge one.

options.name: It is still made of glass
options.effect: A Mimic has no hit points. The first attack that hits it destroys it, exactly like any other Clone, however good the AC it borrowed.

options.name: Half damage still applies
options.effect: Mirror Barrage halves a Clone's damage as normal, including a Mimic's borrowed attack.

features.name: Treacherous Opening
features.description: A borrowed face is a weapon the moment you stop needing it. Once per combat, the first attack roll you make against a creature that currently believes a Perfect Mimicry disguise of yours is genuine is made with advantage and deals an extra [[1d6]] damage on a hit. Making an attack immediately ends the deception for every creature that sees it — the face stays, but nobody believes it anymore.
features.narration: They are still talking to a face they trust when it hits them. That is the whole trick, and it only works once per face, because after that nobody in the room believes anything wearing it.
features.sheetSummary: Your first attack roll against a creature currently fooled by your Perfect Mimicry has advantage and deals an extra [[1d6]] damage on a hit. Attacking ends the deception for every creature that sees it.

subclasses.name: Juggernaut
subclasses.flavor: The offense discipline: a Sandow who never stops moving forward, turning every hit, shove, and thrown body into fuel for the next, bigger swing.

features.name: Unstoppable Force
features.description: You feed on the wreckage you cause. In addition to your baseline Grit generation, you gain 1 additional Grit the first time each turn you deal damage to a creature with a Heave throw, and you gain 1 Grit the first time each turn you knock a creature prone by some means OTHER than a Heave (a shove, Bulldozer Charge, Earthshaker, and the like) — two separate sources, each capped at once per turn, exactly like your baseline Grit generation. A Heave already pays out through the first source, so the prone it also causes never grants a second Grit off the same throw. The bigger the mess you make, the more you have left to make it worse.
features.narration: Wreckage agrees with you. Every body you throw, every thing you put on its back, feeds the next one — you do not tire across a fight, you accumulate.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. On top of baseline Grit: +1 Grit the first time each turn you damage a creature with a Heave throw, and +1 Grit the first time each turn you knock a creature prone by any means other than a Heave. Two sources, each once per turn; a Heave never pays both.

features.name: Bulldozer Charge
features.description: When you move at least 15 feet in a straight line toward a creature and then hit it with a melee weapon attack before the end of the same turn, the attack deals an extra [[1d6]] bludgeoning damage, and the target must succeed on a Strength saving throw against your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}} or be knocked prone and pushed 5 feet directly away from you, your choice of direction. You can use Bulldozer Charge only once per turn.
features.narration: You do not close the distance so much as delete it. Fifteen feet of straight-line acceleration arrives all at once, and whatever it arrives at goes over backwards and slides.
features.sheetSummary: After moving at least 15 ft in a straight line toward a creature and hitting it with a melee weapon attack: extra [[1d6]] bludgeoning, and a Strength save vs your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}} or knocked prone and pushed 5 ft away.

meta.save: Str save vs {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Strength modifier}}

features.name: Through, Not Around
features.description: Doors are a suggestion and walls are a delay. You have advantage on Strength checks made to break, force, or topple objects and barriers, and your attacks deal double damage to objects and structures. Given a minute of uninterrupted battering, you can break through any nonmagical door, palisade, or barricade that a creature of your size could conceivably breach — the only question the table needs to answer is how much noise you make doing it.
features.narration: Doors are a suggestion. Walls are a delay. You have never once looked for the way around something, and given a minute of uninterrupted effort there usually stops being a something.
features.sheetSummary: Advantage on Strength checks to break/force objects and barriers; double damage vs objects and structures. Given 1 minute, breach any breachable nonmagical door or barricade.

subclasses.name: Mirror
subclasses.flavor: The discipline of the counter-strike: a Doppelganger who turns every shattered reflection and every last-second sidestep into consequence for the creature that struck first.

features.name: Shattering Reflection
features.description: Your Clones don't break quietly. Whenever a creature destroys one of your Clones with an attack roll (including a Clone destroyed by an attack redirected onto it via Mirror Image, but never a Clone you destroy yourself through one of your own features), that creature must make a Dexterity saving throw against your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}}. On a failed save, it takes [[1d6+Con]] psychic damage as shards of the shattered illusion rake across it, and it has disadvantage on the next attack roll it makes before the end of its next turn. On a successful save, it takes half as much damage and suffers no other effect. This triggers at most once per turn (no matter how many Clones are destroyed that turn) and requires no action or reaction from you to resolve.
features.narration: Your reflections do not break quietly. Whoever strikes one down is standing far too close when it goes — a hard bright spray of edges, all of them briefly showing that creature its own face, and then not.
features.sheetSummary: Automatic. When a creature destroys one of your Clones with an attack roll (never a Clone you destroy yourself), it makes a Dexterity save vs your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}}. Fail: [[1d6+Con]] psychic and disadvantage on its next attack roll before the end of its next turn. Success: half damage only.

meta.save: Dex save vs {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}}

features.name: Vanishing Trick
features.description: Your Swap doubles as a parting insult, and in a pinch as an escape. It does two separate things:
features.narration: You are gone before the space you left has finished being empty, and the thing nearest it commits to a lunge at nothing. On the occasions you leave it later than that, you trade places with the blow already falling and let the reflection catch what was yours.
features.sheetSummary: Two separate effects, listed below: a free rider on your Swap (1/turn) and a defensive Swap (reaction, 1/combat).

options.name: Parting insult (1/turn, free)
options.effect: When you use Swap, choose one creature within 5 feet of the space you just left that could see you there: it has disadvantage on the next attack roll it makes before the end of your next turn. This costs no action or reaction beyond the Swap itself.

options.name: Defensive Swap (1/combat, reaction)
options.effect: When a creature you can see hits you with an attack, before its damage is dealt, use your reaction to Swap with one of your Clones within Swap's range. You trade places, the blow lands on the Clone now standing where you were and destroys it, and you take no damage.

features.name: Flawless Forgery
features.description: A reflection doesn't have to stay in the glass. As an action, you can create a mirror-copy of a Small or smaller nonmagical object you have held within the last minute. The copy is identical to close inspection but is all surface: it shatters into harmless light if it takes any damage, and dissolves on its own after 1 hour. A forged key opens nothing and a forged coin won't survive a bite test — but for a swap, a con, or a decoy on a cushion, it is perfect. There is no limit on how often you do this — you can maintain **one** forgery at a time, and making a new one crumbles the old.
features.narration: A reflection does not have to stay in the glass. You lift a copy of something you were holding a moment ago — perfect down to the wear on the handle, flawless right up until anybody treats it like a real object.
features.sheetSummary: At will, 1 hour, one forgery at a time. Create a mirror-copy of a Small or smaller nonmagical object you held in the last minute: perfect to inspection, shatters on any damage.

meta.uses: At will, one at a time

subclasses.name: Nightmare
subclasses.flavor: The illusions that stop being entertainment. You do not show them a monster — you show them the one they already had.

features.name: It Gets Worse
features.description: You find the crack in one mind and keep working it. When a creature fails a saving throw against one of your tricks, you can make it your **Subject** — no action required. While a creature is your Subject it makes **every** saving throw against your tricks with disadvantage, for as long as the fight lasts. You can have only one Subject at a time: naming a new one releases the old immediately, and your Subject is released when combat ends. This deliberately never applies to more than one creature at once — the table has exactly one name to remember, however many enemies are in the room.
features.sheetSummary: When a creature fails a save against one of your tricks: it becomes your Subject. Your Subject makes EVERY save against your tricks with disadvantage for the rest of the combat. Only one Subject at a time — naming a new one releases the old, and it ends when combat does.
features.narration: You watched what went through them the first time and you simply do not let it go. Every trick you throw at them after that lands on ground you already broke, and they can feel you choosing them.

features.name: Feed the Fear
features.description: Terror is credibility. The first time each turn a creature fails a saving throw against one of your tricks that deals psychic damage, you gain 1 additional Phantasm, over and above whatever your engine already granted this turn.
features.sheetSummary: Gain 1 additional Phantasm the first time each turn a creature fails a save against one of your psychic-damage tricks.
features.narration: You watch it land and something in you banks it. The scream is not the point. The scream is the receipt.

features.name: Reader of Rooms
features.description: You have spent your career finding the thing an audience is most afraid of and selling it back to them. After a minute of watching or talking to a creature, you learn what it fears most — a person, a memory, a manner of dying, a specific humiliation — as a single clear impression. The creature does not know you have done this. A creature that cannot be frightened yields nothing.
features.sheetSummary: After 1 minute observing or talking to a creature, learn what it fears most as a single clear impression. It doesn't notice. Creatures immune to fear yield nothing.
features.narration: You are not reading minds. You are reading a face across a minute of small talk, the way you have read ten thousand faces from a stage, and by the end of it you know exactly which thing to put in front of them.

subclasses.name: Puppet Master
subclasses.flavor: The offensive discipline of the wire: a Puppeteer who stops treating strung enemies as mere targets and starts treating them as weapons, turning a foe's own momentum, and its own allies, against it.

features.name: Turncoat Strings
features.description: When a hostile creature you have a String attached to hits a target with an attack roll, you can use your reaction to wrench its wire mid-swing, forcing it to make a Strength saving throw against your control DC. On a failure, you redirect the attack toward a different creature of your choice: a creature within the attacker's reach (for a melee attack) or within its range and your line of sight (for a ranged attack). Compare the triggering attack roll to the new target's AC — if it hits, the attack strikes the new target instead (roll its damage against them); if it would miss the new target, the attack misses entirely. On a success, the attack resolves against its original target as normal. You can use Turncoat Strings only once per turn, and it draws on the same reaction as Parry, Disrupting Pull, Guiding Pull, and opportunity attacks — you still get only one reaction per round. This is a single, save-gated redirection of one attack, not a seizure of the creature's turn: it grants you no movement or additional actions from the target the way Grand Marionette does.
features.narration: The swing is already committed when you pull. The arm goes wide, past the target and around into whoever happened to be standing there instead, and the look on its face afterwards is worth more than the damage.
features.sheetSummary: When a hostile Stringed creature hits with an attack, Strength save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}} or you redirect it to another creature within the attacker's reach or range. Compare the original attack roll to the new target's AC. On a save, the attack resolves normally. Uses the same single reaction as Parry.

meta.save: Str save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}

features.name: Puppet's Spite
features.description: Your Control Wires cut deeper into a foe already caught in your web. When you hit a creature you have a String attached to with a Control Wires attack, it takes extra damage equal to your {{Wisdom modifier (min 1)|set from your stats on your character sheet}}. You can deal this extra damage only once per turn. This extra damage applies only to unwilling creatures — it never triggers against a willing creature, such as an ally you've strung for support rather than control.
features.narration: The wire is already inside their guard, so your strike does not have to find a way in — it just follows the line that is already there, into somewhere that was never protected.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. When you hit an unwilling Stringed creature with a Control Wires attack, it takes extra damage equal to your {{Wisdom modifier (min 1)|set from your stats on your character sheet}}. Never triggers against a willing creature.

features.name: Deft Wires
features.description: Your wires are fine enough to vanish in lamplight and precise enough to sign your name. As an action, you can manipulate an object within 30 feet of you as though with your own hands: open a latch, pull a lever, lift or carry up to 10 pounds, pour a drink, palm a key from a belt. Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) checks made this way can target creatures and objects at that range, and you have advantage on them when your hands are visibly elsewhere — nobody suspects the man across the room.
features.narration: Your wires are fine enough to disappear in lamplight and steady enough to sign your name with. Latches lift, levers pull, and a cup crosses a room to your hand with nobody able to say quite how.
features.sheetSummary: Action: manipulate an object within 30 ft as if by hand (open, pull, lift up to 10 lb, pickpocket at range). Advantage on Sleight of Hand made this way while your hands are visibly elsewhere.

subclasses.name: Ringleader
subclasses.flavor: Somebody has to run the show. It was never going to be the strongman. The Ringleader is the Jester who moves everyone else around the stage — the buff-and-debuff discipline, and the only one that never deals damage at all.

features.name: Cue the Next Act
features.description: As a bonus action, choose one ally you can see within 30 feet. It may immediately use its reaction to move up to half its speed without provoking opportunity attacks. You can do this once per combat, and again each time you spend Mirth on a Prestige.
features.sheetSummary: Once per combat (and again whenever you cast a Prestige). One ally may immediately use its reaction to move up to half its speed without provoking opportunity attacks.
features.narration: You call it like a cue, because it is one — a name, a gesture, a stamp of the foot — and they are moving before they have decided to.

features.name: Everyone Watch This
features.description: You point, and one of your people takes the shot. Once on each of your turns, when you cast a Turn that affects one or more enemies, choose one ally you can see within 30 feet: that ally has advantage on its next attack roll against one of those enemies, made before the start of your next turn. **One ally, one attack** — you are handing a single person an opening, not calling the whole company down on one target.
features.sheetSummary: When you cast a Turn affecting one or more enemies, ONE ally of your choice within 30 ft has advantage on its next attack roll against one of those enemies, before the start of your next turn.
features.narration: You call it like a cue and half the room looks where you are pointing — including the one person you actually meant it for, who is already moving.

features.name: Top of the Bill
features.description: You can run a room the way you run a ring. Given 10 minutes, you can organise any crowd of up to fifty ordinary people into doing one simple coordinated thing — clearing a square, forming a line, all looking the other way, moving somewhere together. They will not fight for you and they will not risk their lives, but they will follow a confident person with a plan, and you are always the most confident person present.
features.sheetSummary: Given 10 minutes, organise up to fifty ordinary people into one simple coordinated action (clear a space, form a line, look away, move together). They will not fight or risk their lives for you.
features.narration: You get up on something, you raise your voice into its carrying register, and a frightened mob becomes an audience with a job. It is the same skill as calling an act. It has never once failed to work.

subclasses.name: Ringmaster
subclasses.flavor: The showman: a juggler who works the whole ring, turning heavy clubs and sheer spectacle into crowd control — every eye on him, whether they like it or not.

features.name: All Eyes On Me
features.description: You command attention like a spotlight. Once on each of your turns, when you hit a creature with an implement, you can forgo that implement's damage to instead rivet its attention on you: it must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw against your {{Trick Shot DC|6 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}} or have disadvantage on any attack roll that doesn't include you as a target, until the start of your next turn. You can hold only one creature's attention this way at a time.
features.narration: You catch it with something that does not hurt at all — a club to the chest, a flourish, a bow — and every bit of its attention comes off whoever it was killing and lands on you. That is the job. Now keep it.
features.sheetSummary: Part of your Barrage. On a hit, forgo that implement's damage: Wisdom save vs your {{Trick Shot DC|6 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}} or disadvantage on any attack roll that doesn't include you as a target, until the start of your next turn. One creature at a time.

meta.save: Wis vs Trick Shot DC

features.name: Grand Finale
features.description: Once per combat, you can turn a Barrage into a showstopping set piece. Take the Attack action and throw implements as normal, then put on the show: each ally who can see you gains temporary hit points equal to your Juggler level, and each enemy within 15 feet of you must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw against your {{Trick Shot DC|6 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}} or be frightened of you until the end of its next turn. The crowd is yours.
features.narration: You stop fighting and start performing. The whole cascade goes up at once, the room's eyes come with it, and by the time it comes down your friends are standing straighter and the people trying to kill you have remembered they are afraid.
features.sheetSummary: Part of the Attack action. Throw your Barrage as normal, then each ally who can see you gains temporary hit points equal to your Juggler level, and each enemy within 15 ft makes a Wisdom save vs your {{Trick Shot DC|6 + proficiency bonus + Intelligence modifier}} or is frightened of you until the end of its next turn.

meta.save: Wis vs Trick Shot DC

features.name: Command the Crowd
features.description: The ring taught you that any room is an audience that hasn't been addressed yet. Your voice carries clearly up to 300 feet without shouting. You have advantage on Charisma checks made to address, sway, or intimidate a group of three or more creatures at once, and with a word and a gesture you can pull a nonhostile crowd's attention onto yourself — cutting through noise, panic, or a rival speaker mid-sentence.
features.narration: Any room is an audience that has not been addressed yet. Your voice reaches the back without rising, and a crowd that was about to become a mob turns into a crowd again because you told it to.
features.sheetSummary: Voice carries 300 ft clearly. Advantage on Charisma checks against groups of 3+ creatures. Can seize a nonhostile crowd's attention at will (cuts through noise/panic).

subclasses.name: Swarm
subclasses.flavor: The discipline of overwhelming numbers: a Doppelganger who stops treating a Clone as one spare body and starts fielding a crowd, letting sheer duplication wear a target down from every angle at once.

features.name: Overflowing Reflections
features.description: Your reflections multiply more readily than most. Your Clone cap increases by 1 (this stacks with the increase Hall of Mirrors grants at 5th level). Additionally, once per combat, when you use your bonus action to create a Clone, you may create a second Clone at the same time, provided doing so would not exceed your (increased) Clone cap; both appear following the normal rules for Clone creation, in unoccupied spaces you can see within range.
features.narration: They come faster than they should. You leave one behind and there are somehow two of them standing there, both wearing the expression you had a second ago.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Clone cap +1, stacking with Hall of Mirrors. Once per combat, when you create a Clone with your bonus action, create a second at the same time if that stays within your cap.

features.name: Overwhelming Numbers
features.description: You press your numbers from every angle at once — and then take the legs out. Once per turn, when you hit a creature with a weapon attack while one of your Clones is within 5 feet of it, two things happen: you deal an extra [[1d4]] damage of the weapon's damage type as the creature flinches from a second angle it can't track, and the Clone sweeps in at the same instant, forcing the target to succeed on a Constitution saving throw against your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}} or be knocked prone. Both happen at most once per turn no matter how many Clones are adjacent, and this combines with the advantage granted by Flanking Reflection.
features.narration: They cannot cover every angle because there are more angles than there are of them. You come in from one side while a reflection takes the legs from the other, and the ground arrives before they have worked out which of you did it.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. When you hit a creature with a weapon attack while one of your Clones is within 5 ft of it: extra [[1d4]] damage of the weapon's type, and a Constitution save vs your {{save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Constitution modifier}} or knocked prone. Once per turn however many Clones are adjacent; stacks with Flanking Reflection's advantage.

meta.save: Con save vs your DC (or prone)

features.name: One-Man Crowd
features.description: Why blend into a crowd when you can bring your own? Outside combat, your Clones can wear faces that aren't yours — distinct strangers rather than copies — and can mill about within 60 feet of you: enough to fake a gathering, an entourage, a queue, or a very busy alibi. You have advantage on ability checks made to blend into, start, or read a crowd, and you know instantly when one of your Clones is destroyed, and where it was.
features.narration: Why blend into a crowd when you can bring one? Your reflections wear faces that were never yours, mill about, take up space, and hold a conversation with each other while you do the actual work.
features.sheetSummary: Out of combat, Clones can look like distinct strangers and mill within 60 ft (fake crowds, entourages, alibis). Advantage on checks to blend into/start/read crowds. Know instantly when and where a Clone is destroyed.

subclasses.name: Tangleweaver
subclasses.flavor: The battlefield-control discipline of the wire: a Puppeteer who stops stringing up creatures one at a time and starts filling whole patches of ground with wire, so that walking into the show at all becomes the mistake.

features.name: Snare Weave
features.description: As an action, you weave loose wire across the ground in a 15-foot square within 60 feet of you, filling it with a low, near-invisible lattice that lasts for 1 minute or until you dismiss it (no action required). The area is difficult terrain to any creature without a String attached to you. Any creature other than you that enters the area for the first time on a turn or starts its turn there must succeed on a Strength saving throw against your control DC or become restrained by the wire. A creature restrained this way can repeat the save at the end of each of its turns, ending the restrained condition on itself on a success, or use its action to make a Strength or Dexterity check (its choice) against your control DC to tear free instead. You can use Snare Weave {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} times per combat.
features.narration: You lay wire across the floor in a low, glittering lattice nobody notices until their ankle finds it. Crossing it is a decision; standing in it is a mistake that tightens.
features.sheetSummary: {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} times per combat, 15-ft square within 60 ft, 1 minute. Difficult terrain for anyone without your String. Entering it for the first time on a turn or starting a turn there forces a Strength save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}} or restrained; repeat at the end of each turn, or use an action for a Strength or Dexterity check to tear free.

meta.save: Str save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}

features.name: Binding Knots
features.description: Your bindings compound on themselves. When you use Tangle, you can target one additional creature you have a String attached to within range, provided the two targets are within 15 feet of each other and you don't mix a willing target with an unwilling one in the same use. You can use this double-target option {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} times per combat.
features.narration: One knot pulls the next. The wire you put on one of them runs through the one beside it, and when you cinch it down they both go rigid at once, tangled into each other's mistakes.
features.sheetSummary: Passive with Tangle, {{uses per combat|1 at levels 1-4, 2 at 5-10, 3 at 11-16, 4 at 17+ — the same breakpoints the Scaling Die uses}} times per combat. Tangle may target one additional Stringed creature within 15 ft of the first. Both targets must be willing or both unwilling.

features.name: Wired Room
features.description: You never sleep anywhere you haven't strung first. Over 10 minutes, you can rig an area up to a 30-foot square — a room, a campsite, a corridor — with a lattice of near-invisible trip-lines that lasts 8 hours or until you dismantle it. You know instantly when a Small or larger creature enters the area (and roughly where). When you rig the area, you can include one snare: the first creature to trigger it must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw against your Control DC or be caught, restrained until it or an ally uses an action to cut it free.
features.narration: You have not slept in an unstrung room in years. Ten minutes with the doorways and the corners and the place tells you, in a small tug against your finger, the moment anything crosses it.
features.sheetSummary: 10 min: wire up to a 30-ft square for 8 h — know instantly when a Small or larger creature enters. Optional snare: first trigger, Dex save vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}} or restrained until cut free (action).

meta.save: Dex vs {{control DC|8 + proficiency bonus + Wisdom modifier}}

subclasses.name: Tightrope
subclasses.flavor: The precision discipline: a performer who has spent so long balanced on a single strand of wire high above the crowd that solid ground feels generous, and every strike lands exactly where it was always going to.

features.name: Perfect Balance
features.description: You ignore the effects of narrow, unstable, or slippery surfaces: you can move across a tightrope, ledge, ice, rubble, or similar footing at your full speed, without needing an ability check, and you don't fall from such a surface. Additionally, you have advantage on saving throws and ability checks made to avoid being knocked prone or moved against your will. From 5th level, that unshakeable footing becomes an answer. When a creature within 5 feet of you misses you with an attack roll, you can use your reaction to make one melee weapon attack against it. Like all your weapon attacks (see Improved Critical), this scores a critical hit on a 19 or 20, and on a hit you throw the target off its line: it has disadvantage on the next attack roll it makes before the start of your next turn. This is distinct from your base Riposte, which triggers on a clean Full Dodge and spends Momentum at no reaction cost; this one punishes any miss and costs your reaction. It uses the same single reaction as Parry, so landing both a Parry and this counter in one round relies on Flowing Reflexes (3rd level) returning your reaction after a successful Parry.
features.narration: Ledges, ice, rubble, a rope over a drop — none of it registers as difficult; you simply walk it at speed while everyone else picks their way. And when a strike comes in and misses, your footing was never the thing in question, so you answer from exactly where you were standing.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Ignore narrow, unstable, or slippery footing: full speed, no check, no falling from it. Advantage on saves and checks against being knocked prone or moved against your will. From 5th level, when a creature within 5 ft misses you, use your reaction to make one melee weapon attack against it (critting on 19-20 via Improved Critical); on a hit it has disadvantage on its next attack roll before the start of your next turn. Uses the same single reaction as Parry.

features.name: Improved Critical
features.description: Your weapon attacks score a critical hit on a roll of 19 or 20. Whenever you score a critical hit, you regain 1 Momentum (no more than once per turn, and never above your current cap).
features.narration: You have an eye for the seam — the gap in the plate, the place the guard is thin — and you find it far more often than the odds say you should. Every time you do, it feeds the rhythm.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Your weapon attacks crit on a 19 or 20. On a crit, regain 1 Momentum, no more than once per turn and never above your cap.

features.name: Wire-Walker's Poise
features.description: Years above the crowd have calibrated your eye and your nerve. You can judge any distance, height, drop, or gap you can see to within a foot, just by looking. You have advantage on Charisma (Performance) checks that showcase balance or precision, and you can carry one willing Medium or smaller creature across a narrow or unstable surface without slowing or risking either of you.
features.narration: Years spent above a crowd have calibrated your eye. You can look at a gap, a drop, a span, and simply know it — no pacing it out, no guessing — and you can carry someone across a wire without either of you wobbling, which they will talk about for a long time afterwards.
features.sheetSummary: Judge any visible distance/height/drop exactly by eye. Advantage on balance/precision Performance checks. Carry one willing Medium or smaller creature across narrow surfaces safely at full speed.

subclasses.name: Trapeze
subclasses.flavor: The purest expression of the Acrobat's aerial fantasy: a performer who treats open air as solid ground, closing distance, escaping danger, and pulling allies along for the ride on lines only they can see.

features.name: Aerial Anchor
features.description: Your mastery of the trapeze frees you from needing real rigging. You can use Trapeze Swing at any time, even when no rope, chandelier, banner, or similar structure is within reach, treating open air as your line. Additionally, when you use Trapeze Swing, you may bring one willing or incapacitated Medium or smaller creature within 5 feet of you along the swing; that creature moves with you at no cost to your own movement and does not provoke opportunity attacks during the swing. Trapeze Swing remains a signature move when used this way, so it still generates Momentum. From 5th level, your lines reach anywhere you can see. When a creature you can see within 30 feet of you hits an ally with an attack, you can use your reaction to drop onto a line out of nowhere and swing to an unoccupied space within 5 feet of that attacker, then make one melee weapon attack against it — punishing the opening the instant it commits. As always, this aerial style is flashy, not safe: leaving a creature's reach as you swing provokes opportunity attacks as normal. It does not count as your Trapeze Swing for the turn and generates no Momentum. It uses the same single reaction as Parry, so on a turn when Flowing Reflexes (3rd level) returns your reaction after a clean Parry, you can both defend yourself and swing to a struck ally's aid in the same round.
features.narration: You do not need rigging any more; open air is a line if you decide it is. You take passengers now, and when something goes after a friend across the room you drop out of nowhere on a line that was not there, arriving between them.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. Trapeze Swing needs no real rigging — open air works. When you Swing you may bring one willing or incapacitated Medium or smaller creature within 5 ft along, at no cost to your movement and without it provoking. From 5th level, when a creature within 30 ft hits an ally, use your reaction to swing to a space within 5 ft of it and make one melee weapon attack; leaving reach still provokes. Doesn't count as your Trapeze Swing and generates no Momentum.

features.name: Featherweight Landing
features.description: Your body has learned to always find purchase. You take no damage from a fall of 30 feet or less, and for any longer fall you calculate damage as though you had fallen 30 feet less than you actually did. In addition, whenever you fall or would be knocked prone as a result of your own fall or your own signature move (such as a failed Wall-Run or Trapeze Swing), you can spend 1 Momentum (no action required) to land on your feet instead, ending the fall without becoming prone, provided you end it in a space you could normally occupy. This does not apply to being knocked prone or forcibly moved by a hostile creature's attack, spell, or ability.
features.narration: Your body has stopped believing in falling. Long drops end with a soft roll and a stand, and even the ones that go wrong — a slipped wall-run, a swing that came apart — end with your feet under you and your hands out as though it was choreography.
features.sheetSummary: Passive. No damage from a fall of 30 ft or less; longer falls count as 30 ft shorter. When you fall or would be knocked prone by your own fall or your own signature move, spend 1 Momentum (no action) to land on your feet in a space you could occupy. Never applies to a hostile creature's attack, spell, or ability.

features.name: Show Rigging
features.description: The lines you conjure don't have to be for you alone. As an action outside combat, you can conjure up to 60 feet of shimmering rigging anchored to any two points you can see — a climbable rope, a rope ladder, or a taut line. It holds up to 500 pounds, lasts 10 minutes or until you dismiss it (no action required), and you can maintain only one at a time. You also have advantage on ability checks involving ropes, knots, and rigging.
features.narration: The lines are not only for you. You conjure rope, ladder, and taut line out of nothing, anchored to two points nobody thought were connected, and the whole party goes up.
features.sheetSummary: Action (out of combat): conjure up to 60 ft of climbable rigging between two visible anchor points (holds 500 lb, lasts 10 min, one at a time). Advantage on rope/knot/rigging checks.

subclasses.name: Trickster
subclasses.flavor: Every illusion is misdirection with better staging. You cut out the staging.

features.name: Two Places at Once
features.description: When you use Misdirection to move after casting a trick, you can spend 1 Phantasm to leave a silent, motionless illusory double of yourself standing in the space you left. Until the start of your next turn, the first attack roll made against you is made with **disadvantage** — the attacker commits to the wrong one of you before it can tell which is breathing. The double then vanishes, whether or not anyone swung at it. It is only ever an image: it has no space of its own that matters, it cannot be attacked, and nobody ever has to work out which of the two of you they are targeting.
features.sheetSummary: Costs 1 Phantasm, when Misdirection moves you. Leave a motionless illusory double in the space you left: the FIRST attack roll against you before the start of your next turn is made with disadvantage, then the double vanishes. No targeting choice for anyone to make.
features.narration: You step away and something stays — the same coat, the same posture, holding perfectly still where you were a moment ago. Whoever swings next has to decide, in the time it takes to swing, and they get it wrong.

features.name: Palmed
features.description: Hide the real work inside the loud work: once on each of your turns, when you cast a Turn, you may also cast one Pledge as part of the same action. The Pledge resolves after the Turn. With Palmed Card in your list this is a second attack every round for nothing, which is the whole reason to take this discipline.
features.sheetSummary: When you cast a Turn, also cast one Pledge as part of the same action; the Pledge resolves after the Turn.
features.narration: The big gesture is the cover. The small one, the one that actually matters, happens inside it while everyone is busy applauding the wrong hand.

features.name: Second Nature
features.description: Sleight of hand has stopped requiring your attention. You can palm, plant, swap, or produce any object small enough to fit in one hand without being noticed, with no check, provided nobody is deliberately watching your hands. Against a creature that IS watching your hands, you have advantage on the check. You can also perform any Pledge without any visible gesture at all, so nobody can tell you cast anything.
features.sheetSummary: Palm, plant, swap, or produce a hand-sized object with no check. A creature deliberately watching your hands makes it a Sleight of Hand check at advantage instead. You can cast any Pledge with no visible somatic component.
features.narration: The hands do it without being asked any more. You have handed back a stolen ring while apologising for the theft and nobody in the room, including the owner, saw either half.

subclasses.name: Warden
subclasses.flavor: The protective discipline of the wire: a Puppeteer who strings up allies not to move them like pieces on a board, but to hold a line back to them, ready to snap taut the instant one is struck.

features.name: Warding Pull
features.description: When a creature you have a String attached to is hit by an attack, you can use your reaction to snap its wire taut, guiding it half a step aside at the last instant and granting it resistance to the damage from that attack. This draws on the same reaction as Parry, Disrupting Pull, and Guiding Pull — you still get only one reaction per round, so protecting an ally this way costs the same reaction you'd otherwise spend defending yourself or disrupting a foe.
features.narration: The blow is landing and there is no time to stop it, so you do not — you snap the wire and move them half a step into it instead, turning something that would have gone through them into something that only glances.
features.sheetSummary: Within leash. When a Stringed creature is hit by an attack, grant it resistance to that attack's damage. Uses the same single reaction as Parry.

features.name: Steadfast Line
features.description: A willing creature you have a String attached to has advantage on saving throws made to avoid being knocked prone or forcibly moved, as long as it remains within your leash range — your wire keeps it steady on its feet. Additionally, if such a creature is knocked prone anyway, it can spend only 5 feet of movement (instead of half its speed) to stand back up, guided upright by the string.
features.narration: There is a line on them and the line does not let go. Shoves land and they stay upright, and if they do go down the wire has them on their feet again almost before they have finished falling.
features.sheetSummary: Passive, within leash. A willing Stringed creature has advantage on saves against being knocked prone or forcibly moved, and needs only 5 ft of movement to stand up from prone.

features.name: Keeper's Thread
features.description: Some strings aren't for pulling — they're for holding on. Over 1 minute, you can tie a hair-fine thread to a willing creature you touch. For the next 24 hours, while the creature is within 1 mile of you, you know its direction and its general condition (unharmed, wounded, unconscious, or dead), and if it is in danger while you sleep, the thread's tug wakes you instantly. You can maintain a number of threads equal to your {{Wisdom modifier (min 1)|set from your stats on your character sheet}}.
features.narration: Some strings are not for pulling. A hair-fine thread, tied in a quiet minute, and for a day afterwards you know which way they are and roughly how they are doing — and if something goes badly wrong out there, you are awake before you know why.
features.sheetSummary: 1-minute ritual, one willing creature, 24 hours. Know its direction and rough condition (unharmed, wounded, unconscious, dead) within 1 mile, and its danger wakes you from sleep. Hold {{Wisdom modifier (min 1)|set from your stats on your character sheet}} threads at once.

tricks.name: After-Image
tricks.flavor: For half a heartbeat the thing sees itself standing where it was a moment ago — and the copy is already swinging.
tricks.description: You peel a creature's own reflection off it, a half-second behind and a half-step wrong, and let it strike. Make a {{trick attack|d20 + proficiency bonus + your trick ability modifier}} against a creature you can see within range; on a hit it takes [[1d6]] psychic damage as its body flinches from a blow its eyes swear it already took. The after-image is a fleeting image with no substance: it is not a Clone, it occupies no space, it cannot be attacked or interacted with, and it is gone before your turn ends. Because this is an attack roll and not a saving throw, it can be parried like any other attack.
tricks.narration: You catch the edge of its own reflection and peel it off — a half-second behind, a half-step wrong — and let the copy swing. The blow it takes is one it has already watched itself take, and the body flinches from a wound that never opened.
tricks.sheetSummary: Ranged trick attack ({{trick attack|d20 + proficiency bonus + your trick ability modifier}}). Hit: [[1d6]] psychic. Scales at 5/11/17. Creates no Clone. Can be parried.

tricks.name: Bad Beat
tricks.flavor: Nothing you did. The rope was always frayed, the flagstone was always loose, and this was always the moment.
tricks.description: You call the odds against one creature you can see within range and let them arrive. It makes a Dexterity saving throw against your {{trick save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + your trick ability modifier}}. On a failure it takes [[2d6]] physical damage as something around it gives way — footing, fitting, its own weapon's grip — and it is knocked prone. On a success it takes half as much damage and stays on its feet. Casting this costs 1 Mirth, spent as you cast; like every costed Turn it generates none back.
tricks.narration: You do not touch it and you do not point. You just say something that turns out to be true a half-second later, and the world does the rest.
tricks.sheetSummary: Dexterity save vs {{trick save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + your trick ability modifier}}. Fail: [[2d6]] physical and knocked prone. Success: half damage, not prone.

tricks.name: Bad Break
tricks.flavor: "Ooh, unlucky," you say, tutting — and somehow you're right.
tricks.castingTime: 1 reaction, which you take when a creature you can see within range makes an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw
tricks.description: You click your tongue at exactly the wrong moment, and the universe agrees with you. When a creature you can see within range makes an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw, you can force it to reroll and use the lower of the two results. You can use this trick after the original roll is seen but before its effect (hit or miss, success or failure) is determined.
tricks.narration: "Ooh — unlucky," you say, tutting, at exactly the wrong moment. The universe, for reasons of its own, agrees with you.
tricks.sheetSummary: Force a seen d20 roll (attack, check, or save) to be made twice; the lower result is used.

tricks.name: Card Trick
tricks.flavor: A flick of the wrist and the top card leaves the deck edge-first, humming, sharp enough to open a throat.
tricks.description: You snap a razor-edged card at a creature you can see within range. Make a {{trick attack|d20 + proficiency bonus + your trick ability modifier}} against the target; on a hit it takes [[1d6]] slashing damage. Because this is an attack roll and not a saving throw, it can be parried like any other attack.
tricks.narration: A flick of the wrist and the top card leaves the deck edge-first, humming as it goes. It should be paper. It arrives like a razor.
tricks.sheetSummary: Ranged trick attack ({{trick attack|d20 + proficiency bonus + your trick ability modifier}}). Hit: [[1d6]] slashing. Scales at 5/11/17. Can be parried.

tricks.name: Center Ring
tricks.flavor: You do not want the spotlight. You have never wanted the spotlight. But you know exactly where to point it, and the whole room follows your hand.
tricks.description: You throw the spotlight onto a pairing of your choosing. Choose one creature you can see within range and one other creature you can see — the one you want it dealing with. The target makes a Wisdom saving throw against your {{trick save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + your trick ability modifier}}. On a failure, until the start of your next turn it must direct its next attack, trick, or other harmful single-target effect at the creature you named, if that creature is a legal target for it; if it is not, the effect simply lapses for that action. **This changes who it aims at, nothing else:** it makes its own attack roll against the named creature's AC as normal, and can miss, exactly as with the Puppeteer's Turncoat Strings. You cannot name yourself — the Jester books the act, he does not headline it.
tricks.narration: You gesture the way a ringmaster gestures, and the thing turns to look at whoever is standing at the end of your arm. It was going to hurt somebody anyway. Now it is going to hurt the one wearing armour.
tricks.sheetSummary: Name a target and another creature you can see. Wisdom save vs {{trick save DC|8 + proficiency bonus + your trick ability modifier}} or, until the start of your next turn, it must aim its next attack or harmful single-target effect at the creature you named, if legal. It still rolls its attack against that creature's AC as normal and can miss. You can never name yourself.

tricks.name: Cut the Strings
tricks.flavor: A snip of the fingers on a wire you already laid, and whatever was holding them up simply isn't.
